## Loading the packages we need:

```{r}
#| label: Package Setup

library(readr)
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
```

## File paths for the dataset folders:

```{r}
#| label: File-Path Declarations

directory <- "../Datasets/"
cleaned_directory <- "../Datasets/Cleaned/" #Cleaned Datasets get stored here
dir.create(cleaned_directory, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

# 1. Data Import, Structure and Selection

## 1.1 Import with explicit column types

**Problem:** `HouseholdID` is an 18-digit number. R stores numbers as doubles, which are only exact up to about 15–16 digits, so letting `read_csv()` guess the type rounds the IDs (Milestone 1, section 8.3). `PersonNumber` is stored as "01", "02", … and must have the same type in every file for joins to match. `EducationAttendanceCode` and `MinutesToWork` contain text placeholders mixed into numeric codes.

**Treatment:** read every file with explicit types: IDs as text (`col_character()`) in all four files, and the two contaminated columns as text so no value is silently lost. `clean_names()` converts all column names to snake_case. The datasets are named D01, D02, D03 and D08, as in the ERD and the EDA, and are cleaned step by step under the same names. A summary of each uncleaned dataset is recorded in 1.2, before anything changes, for the before/after comparisons.

```{r}
#| label: Import Datasets

D01 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D01_Population_Profile.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character(), PersonNumber = col_character())) |> clean_names()

D02 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D02_Learning_Profile.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character(), PersonNumber = col_character(), EducationAttendanceCode = col_character())) |> clean_names()

D03 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D03_Economic_Participation.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character(), PersonNumber = col_character(),MinutesToWork = col_character())) |> clean_names()

D08 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D08_Connectivity_Access.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character())) |> clean_names()
```

**Verification:** no parsing problems, IDs stored as text with all 18 digits intact.

```{r}
#| label: Verify Imports

tibble(
  
  dataset = c("D01", "D02", "D03", "D08"),
  
  parsing_problems = c(nrow(problems(D01)), nrow(problems(D02)), nrow(problems(D03)), nrow(problems(D08))),
  
  household_id_type = c(class(D01$household_id), class(D02$household_id), class(D03$household_id), class(D08$household_id)),
  
  shortest_id = c(min(nchar(D01$household_id), na.rm = TRUE), min(nchar(D02$household_id)), min(nchar(D03$household_id)), min(nchar(D08$household_id))),
  
  longest_id = c(max(nchar(D01$household_id), na.rm = TRUE), max(nchar(D02$household_id)), max(nchar(D03$household_id)), max(nchar(D08$household_id))),
  
  distinct_households = c(n_distinct(D01$household_id, na.rm = TRUE), n_distinct(D02$household_id), n_distinct(D03$household_id), n_distinct(D08$household_id)),
  
  distinct_if_stored_as_number = c(n_distinct(as.numeric(D01$household_id), na.rm = TRUE), n_distinct(as.numeric(D02$household_id)), n_distinct(as.numeric(D03$household_id)), n_distinct(as.numeric(D08$household_id)))
  
)
```

**Effect:** the last column shows what would have happened without this treatment. Stored as numbers, D08's `r format(n_distinct(D08$household_id), big.mark = ",")` distinct households would collapse to `r format(n_distinct(as.numeric(D08$household_id)), big.mark = ",")`, merging different households together. This is exactly the count behind the EDA's 98.77% household match, so that figure was caused by the rounding problem rather than by missing households. As text, every ID keeps all 18 digits.

## 1.2 Uncleaned "before" summary

**Problem:** the rubric requires before-and-after evidence for every major preprocessing decision.

**Treatment:** record the size, missing values, key uniqueness and duplicates of each uncleaned dataset in `uncleaned_summary`, so the later sections can compare the cleaned data against the uncleaned data.

```{r}
#| label: Uncleaned Datasets Summary

uncleaned_summary <- tibble(
  
  dataset = c("D01", "D02", "D03", "D08"),
  
  rows = c(nrow(D01), nrow(D02), nrow(D03), nrow(D08)),
  
  cols = c(ncol(D01), ncol(D02), ncol(D03), ncol(D08)),
  
  missing_values = c(sum(is.na(D01)), sum(is.na(D02)), sum(is.na(D03)), sum(is.na(D08))),
  
  missing_household_id = c(sum(is.na(D01$household_id)), sum(is.na(D02$household_id)),sum(is.na(D03$household_id)), sum(is.na(D08$household_id))),
  
  distinct_keys = c(nrow(distinct(D01, household_id, person_number)), nrow(distinct(D02, household_id, person_number)),
                    nrow(distinct(D03, household_id, person_number)), n_distinct(D08$household_id)),
  
  exact_duplicate_rows = c(nrow(D01) - nrow(distinct(D01)), nrow(D02) - nrow(distinct(D02)),
                           nrow(D03) - nrow(distinct(D03)), nrow(D08) - nrow(distinct(D08)))
  
)
uncleaned_summary
```

Columns with missing values in each uncleaned dataset:

```{r}
#| label: Missing Values in Datasets


bind_rows(
  D01 = enframe(colSums(is.na(D01)), name = "column", value = "missing"),
  D02 = enframe(colSums(is.na(D02)), name = "column", value = "missing"),
  D03 = enframe(colSums(is.na(D03)), name = "column", value = "missing"),
  D08 = enframe(colSums(is.na(D08)), name = "column", value = "missing"),
  .id = "dataset"
) |>
  filter(missing > 0) |> #Only show columns that have missing values
  left_join(select(uncleaned_summary, dataset, rows), by = "dataset") |>
  mutate(percent_of_rows = round(missing / rows * 100, 2))
```

## 1.3 Grain and key checks

**Problem:** before any join, the unit of observation (grain) and the key of every dataset must be confirmed, and it must be shown that the datasets can legitimately be linked.

**Treatment:** compare row counts with distinct keys, and check how many households each selected dataset shares with D01.

```{r}
#| label: Grain Check/Verification

D01_repeated_keys <- D01 |> filter(!is.na(household_id)) |> count(household_id, person_number) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()
D02_repeated_keys <- D02 |> count(household_id, person_number) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()
D03_repeated_keys <- D03 |> count(household_id, person_number) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()
D08_repeated_keys <- D08 |> count(household_id) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()

tibble(
  
  dataset = c("D01", "D02", "D03", "D08"),
  
  grain = c("person", "person", "person", "household"),
  
  key = c("household_id + person_number", "household_id + person_number", "household_id + person_number", "household_id"),
  
  rows = c(nrow(D01), nrow(D02), nrow(D03), nrow(D08)),
  
  distinct_keys = c(nrow(distinct(filter(D01, !is.na(household_id)), household_id, person_number)), nrow(distinct(D02, household_id, person_number)), nrow(distinct(D03, household_id, person_number)), n_distinct(D08$household_id)),
  
  keys_appearing_more_than_once = c(D01_repeated_keys, D02_repeated_keys, D03_repeated_keys, D08_repeated_keys),
  
  rows_missing_household_id = c(sum(is.na(D01$household_id)), sum(is.na(D02$household_id)), sum(is.na(D03$household_id)), sum(is.na(D08$household_id)))
  
)
```

```{r}
#| label: Shared Households Check

D01_households <- unique(na.omit(D01$household_id)) #Distinct household IDs in D01

tibble(

  compared_with = c("D02", "D03", "D08"),

  households_in_dataset = c(n_distinct(D02$household_id), n_distinct(D03$household_id), n_distinct(D08$household_id)),

  shared_with_D01 = c(length(intersect(D01_households, D02$household_id)), length(intersect(D01_households, D03$household_id)), length(intersect(D01_households, D08$household_id))),
  
  percent_of_D01 = round(shared_with_D01 / length(D01_households) * 100, 2)
  
)
```

```{r}
#| label: People per Household Check

D01 |>
  filter(!is.na(household_id)) |>
  count(household_id, name = "persons") |>
  summarise(households = n(), mean_persons = round(mean(persons), 2), median_persons = median(persons), max_persons = max(persons))
```

**Effect / Verification:** D01, D02 and D03 are one row per person and D08 is exactly one row per household (`r format(nrow(D08), big.mark = ",")` rows, `r format(n_distinct(D08$household_id), big.mark = ",")` distinct IDs). All `r format(length(D01_households), big.mark = ",")` D01 households appear in D02, D03 and D08 (100%). This corrects the 98.77% reported in the EDA: its count of `r format(n_distinct(as.numeric(D08$household_id)), big.mark = ",")` is the number of distinct IDs left after rounding (step 1.1). Household IDs repeat in the person files because a household contains several people. These are legitimate repeats in a one-to-many relationship, not duplicates. The keys that appear more than once in D02 and D03, and the missing IDs in D01, are treated in 2.1 and 2.2.

## 1.4 Datasets not selected

**Problem:** eleven datasets are available, but a dataset should only be used if it measures a link in the research pathway (digital access → education → employment) and can be linked to the same people at the chosen grain: one row per person, identified by `household_id` + `person_number`. Using a dataset that fails either test adds variables with no role in the analysis, or attaches records to the wrong people.

The seven datasets not selected in Task 1 are read here only to document why they are not used:

```{r}
#| label: Datasets Not Selected

D04 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D04_Dwelling_Conditions.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character())) |> clean_names()

D05 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D05_Basic_Services.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character())) |> clean_names()

D06 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D06_Household_Energy.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character())) |> clean_names()

D07 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D07_Household_Wellbeing.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character())) |> clean_names()

D09 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D09_Household_Resources.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character())) |> clean_names()

D10 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D10_Mobility_Access.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character())) |> clean_names()

#D11 is large, so only its keys and quarter are read in full; its column names are read from the header
D11 <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D11_Labour_Market.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_select = c(HouseholdID, PersonNumber, Quarter),
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) |> clean_names()

D11_columns <- read_csv(file.path(directory, "D11_Labour_Market.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, n_max = 0) |> clean_names() |> names()

tibble(

  dataset = c("D04", "D05", "D06", "D07", "D09", "D10", "D11"),

  measures = c("Dwelling type, materials and condition", "Water and sanitation", "Electricity and energy use",
               "Food security and household income", "Income sources and household assets",
               "Public transport and access to health facilities", "Employment, education and occupation"),

  grain = c("household", "household", "household", "household", "household", "household", "person per quarter"),

  rows = c(nrow(D04), nrow(D05), nrow(D06), nrow(D07), nrow(D09), nrow(D10), nrow(D11)),

  distinct_households = c(n_distinct(D04$household_id), n_distinct(D05$household_id), n_distinct(D06$household_id),
                          n_distinct(D07$household_id), n_distinct(D09$household_id), n_distinct(D10$household_id),
                          n_distinct(D11$household_id)),

  households_shared_with_D01 = c(length(intersect(D01_households, D04$household_id)),
                                 length(intersect(D01_households, D05$household_id)),
                                 length(intersect(D01_households, D06$household_id)),
                                 length(intersect(D01_households, D07$household_id)),
                                 length(intersect(D01_households, D09$household_id)),
                                 length(intersect(D01_households, D10$household_id)),
                                 length(intersect(D01_households, D11$household_id))),

  reason_not_selected = c("Not a link in the pathway", "Not a link in the pathway", "Not a link in the pathway",
                          "Not in the pathway; household income partly reveals the employment outcome",
                          "Salary income reveals the employment outcome; computer_asset_code duplicates D08",
                          "Not a link in the pathway",
                          "Different sample: cannot be linked to any person in D01")
)
```

D09's only digital-access column is a copy of the one already selected from D08:

```{r}
#| label: D09 Computer Column Check

D09 |>
  distinct(household_id, computer_asset_code_d09 = computer_asset_code) |>
  inner_join(select(D08, household_id, computer_asset_code), by = "household_id") |>
  summarise(households_compared = n(), values_that_differ_from_D08 = sum(computer_asset_code_d09 != computer_asset_code))
```

D11 is the only unselected dataset that measures the employment outcome, so the reasons it cannot be joined are checked directly:

```{r}
#| label: D11 Linkage Check

tibble(
  check = c("rows in D11",
            "distinct people in D11",
            "people recorded in more than one quarter",
            "households shared with D01",
            "PSUs (sampling areas) shared with D01",
            "digital-access columns in D11"),

  result = c(nrow(D11),
             nrow(distinct(D11, household_id, person_number)),
             sum(count(D11, household_id, person_number)$n > 1),
             length(intersect(D11$household_id, D01_households)),
             length(intersect(str_sub(D11$household_id, 1, 11), str_sub(D01_households, 1, 11))), #First 11 digits of an ID = PSU (2.1)
             length(str_subset(D11_columns, "internet|phone|computer")))
)

#Levels of geography at which D11 could be linked to the four selected datasets
selected_columns <- c(names(D01), names(D02), names(D03), names(D08))

tibble(
  geography_level = c("province", "geography type", "metro area"),

  column_in_D11 = c(any(str_detect(D11_columns, "province")), any(str_detect(D11_columns, "geo_type")), any(str_detect(D11_columns, "metro"))),

  column_in_selected_datasets = c(any(str_detect(selected_columns, "province")), any(str_detect(selected_columns, "geo_type")),
                                  any(str_detect(selected_columns, "metro")))
)
```

D11 shares only province and geography type with the selected datasets. It has no metro column, and its PSUs never match D01's (table above), so province and geography type are the most detailed levels at which D11 could be linked to our people.

**Treatment:** select only D01, D02, D03 and D08, and remove the other seven from memory.

- **D04, D05, D06, D07, D09 and D10** are household-level and share almost every household with D01, so they could technically be joined many-to-one. They are left out because of the topic, not because they cannot be linked. Dwelling conditions, water, energy and public transport are not links between digital access, education and employment. Household income (D07, D09) and salary income sources (D09) partly reveal whether someone in the household is employed, so they would leak the outcome. D09's only digital-access column duplicates D08's. D04, D07 and D09 also contain repeated household rows, which would duplicate people if joined without treatment.
- **D11** would be useful, because it records employment status and education for working-age people. It cannot be integrated at the person grain, however. It shares no households and not even a single PSU with D01, so it is a separate sample of different people, not extra information about ours. Its rows are person-quarters, not persons: most people appear in more than one quarter, with separate quarterly and annual weights. The only way to join it would be to match people on shared characteristics such as province, age and sex, which would attach one person's labour-market record to a different person. This is exactly the misalignment that invalid joins create.
- **Aggregation is not a useful alternative for D11 in this topic.** The only geography D11 shares with D01 is province and geography type. A D11 rate aggregated to province and attached to each person would be fully determined by `province_code`, which D01 already contains, so it adds no information at the person level. D11 also has no digital-access columns, so a parallel analysis could only repeat the education → employment link and could not test digital access or its moderating role.

```{r}
#| label: Remove Unselected Datasets

rm(D04, D05, D06, D07, D09, D10, D11, D11_columns, selected_columns) #Only needed for the checks above
```

**Effect / Verification:** the tables confirm the decision. All six household datasets share almost all of D01's households, so their exclusion is a topic decision. D09's computer column never differs from D08's, and D11 shares 0 households and 0 PSUs with D01. The rest of the pipeline cleans and integrates only D01, D02, D03 and D08 (section 9). The employment outcome comes from a single source (D03), which is recorded as a limitation.

# 2. Data Cleaning

## 2.1 Recover the missing household IDs in D01

**Problem:** `r sum(is.na(D01$household_id))` rows in D01 have a missing `household_id`. These people cannot be linked to their education, employment or household connectivity. Exactly the same number of people appear in D03 (and D02) but not in D01, which suggests these are the same people with their ID blanked out.

**Treatment:** match each D01 row with a missing ID to one of the people missing from D01, using `person_number`, `sex_code`, `province_code` and `person_weight`. The survey weight is identical for the same person across D01–D03 and has thousands of distinct values, so it is highly specific. The match is then checked with two attributes that were **not** used to match: the PSU (sampling cluster) must equal the first 11 digits of the recovered household ID, and the age must agree with D03.

```{r}
#| label: Identify Missing People

D01_key_duplicates_before <- get_dupes(D01, household_id, person_number) 

missing_from_D01 <- D03 |>
  distinct() |>
  anti_join(filter(D01, !is.na(household_id)), by = c("household_id", "person_number")) |> 
  select(household_id, person_number, sex_code, province_code, person_weight, age_d03 = age)

rows_missing_id <- D01 |>
  mutate(row_id = row_number()) |> 
  filter(is.na(household_id)) |>
  select(-household_id)

recovered <- rows_missing_id |>
  inner_join(missing_from_D01, by = c("person_number", "sex_code", "province_code", "person_weight"))
```

**Verification:** every D01 row with a missing ID matches exactly one person, every candidate is used exactly once, and both independent checks agree for every match.

```{r}
#| label: Verification of Missing People 

tibble(
  
  D01_rows_missing_id = nrow(rows_missing_id),
  
  people_missing_from_D01 = nrow(missing_from_D01),
  
  matches_found = nrow(recovered),
  
  each_d01_row_matched_once = n_distinct(recovered$row_id) == nrow(rows_missing_id),
  
  each_person_used_once = nrow(distinct(recovered, household_id, person_number)) == nrow(recovered),
  
  psu_agrees_with_id = sum(sprintf("%.0f", recovered$psu) == str_sub(recovered$household_id, 1, 11)), 
  
  age_agrees_with_D03 = sum(recovered$age == recovered$age_d03, na.rm = TRUE)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: Recover Missing People

  D01 <- D01 |> mutate(row_id = row_number()) |>
  left_join(select(recovered, row_id, recovered_id = household_id), by = "row_id") |> 
  
  mutate(household_id_flag = if_else(is.na(household_id) & !is.na(recovered_id), "recovered by matching to D03", NA_character_), household_id =  coalesce(household_id, recovered_id)) |> select(-row_id, -recovered_id)

tibble(
  
  missing_household_id_before = uncleaned_summary$missing_household_id[1], 

  missing_household_id_after = sum(is.na(D01$household_id)),
  
  rows_before = uncleaned_summary$rows[1],
  
  rows_after = nrow(D01),
  
  D01_keys_identical_to_D02 = setequal(paste(D01$household_id, D01$person_number), paste(D02$household_id, D02$person_number))
  
)
```

**Effect:** all `r nrow(recovered)` IDs are recovered with no rows added or removed, and D01 now contains exactly the same set of people as D02. Recovered rows are marked in `household_id_flag`.

## 2.2 Duplicates

**Problem:** the EDA found `r nrow(D01_key_duplicates_before)` (D01), `r nrow(get_dupes(D02, household_id, person_number))` (D02) and `r nrow(get_dupes(D03, household_id, person_number))` (D03) rows sharing a person key. These must be separated into genuine duplicate records (the same record entered twice) and legitimate repeated identifiers.

**Investigation:** every one of D01's key "duplicates" had a missing household ID. Rows with a missing ID and the same person number were grouped together, even though they are different people.

```{r}
#| label: False Duplicates in D01

D01_key_duplicates_before |> count(household_id_missing = is.na(household_id), name = "rows")
```

After the recovery in 2.1, check each dataset for exact copies (every column identical) and for keys that still repeat with different values (conflicts):

```{r}
#| label: Duplicate Check

#Rows that share their key with at least one other row
D01_key_duplicate_rows <- nrow(get_dupes(D01, household_id, person_number))
D02_key_duplicate_rows <- nrow(get_dupes(D02, household_id, person_number))
D03_key_duplicate_rows <- nrow(get_dupes(D03, household_id, person_number))
D08_key_duplicate_rows <- nrow(get_dupes(D08, household_id))

#Exact copies: rows where every column is identical to another row
D01_exact_duplicates <- nrow(D01) - nrow(distinct(D01))
D02_exact_duplicates <- nrow(D02) - nrow(distinct(D02))
D03_exact_duplicates <- nrow(D03) - nrow(distinct(D03))
D08_exact_duplicates <- nrow(D08) - nrow(distinct(D08))

#Keys that still repeat once exact copies are removed, meaning the same person with conflicting values
D01_conflicting_keys <- distinct(D01) |> count(household_id, person_number) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()
D02_conflicting_keys <- distinct(D02) |> count(household_id, person_number) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()
D03_conflicting_keys <- distinct(D03) |> count(household_id, person_number) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()
D08_conflicting_keys <- distinct(D08) |> count(household_id) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()

tibble(
  
  dataset = c("D01", "D02", "D03", "D08"),
  
  rows_before = c(nrow(D01), nrow(D02), nrow(D03), nrow(D08)),
  
  rows_in_key_duplicate_groups = c(D01_key_duplicate_rows, D02_key_duplicate_rows, D03_key_duplicate_rows, D08_key_duplicate_rows),
  
  exact_duplicate_rows = c(D01_exact_duplicates, D02_exact_duplicates, D03_exact_duplicates, D08_exact_duplicates),
  
  conflicting_keys_after_removing_exact_copies = c(D01_conflicting_keys, D02_conflicting_keys, D03_conflicting_keys, D08_conflicting_keys)
)
```

**Treatment:** every key duplicate in D02 and D03 is an exact copy of another row, with no conflicting values, so they are genuine duplicate records. Exact copies are removed with `distinct()`. D01 and D08 contain none.

```{r}
#| label: Remove Duplicates

D01 <- distinct(D01)
D02 <- distinct(D02)
D03 <- distinct(D03)
D08 <- distinct(D08)

tibble(
  dataset = c("D01", "D02", "D03", "D08"),
  
  rows_before = uncleaned_summary$rows,
  
  rows_after = c(nrow(D01), nrow(D02), nrow(D03), nrow(D08)),
  
  rows_removed = rows_before - rows_after,
  
  keys_unique_after = c(nrow(distinct(D01, household_id, person_number)) == nrow(D01), nrow(distinct(D02, household_id, person_number)) == nrow(D02), nrow(distinct(D03, household_id, person_number)) == nrow(D03), n_distinct(D08$household_id) == nrow(D08))
)
```

**Effect / Verification:** D02 loses `r D02_exact_duplicates` rows and D03 loses `r D03_exact_duplicates`. All three person datasets now contain exactly `r format(nrow(D01), big.mark = ",")` people, and every key is unique in every dataset. Repeated `household_id` values remain in the person files, because they are legitimate: one household, several people.

## 2.3 Text placeholders and data types

**Problem:** a code column should contain only numbers. Listing the text columns in each dataset shows which columns contain text where codes are expected (the `_flag` columns created in this pipeline are text by design and are left out):

```{r}
#| label: Text Columns Explanation

bind_rows(
  D01 = enframe(sapply(D01, class), name = "column", value = "type"),
  D02 = enframe(sapply(D02, class), name = "column", value = "type"),
  D03 = enframe(sapply(D03, class), name = "column", value = "type"),
  D08 = enframe(sapply(D08, class), name = "column", value = "type"),
  .id = "dataset"
) |>
  filter(type == "character", !str_ends(column, "_flag")) |> 
  group_by(column) |>
  summarise(datasets = paste(dataset, collapse = ", ")) |> 
  mutate(why_text = case_when(
    column %in% c("household_id", "person_number") ~ "Key, read as text on purpose in 1.1",
    column == "province" ~ "Province name (rebuilt from province_code, dropped in section 3)",
    TRUE ~ "Code column containing text placeholders"
  ))
```

Apart from IDs and the province name, only two columns are text: `education_attendance_code` (D02, kept) and `minutes_to_work` (D03, dropped as leakage in section 3, so it is not treated). `education_attendance_code` mixes numeric codes with three text placeholders, the same problem Milestone 1 found in D11's `hours_worked_raw`:

```{r}
#| label: Initial Student Attendance

D02 |> count(education_attendance_code)
```

None of the placeholders appears in the data dictionary. "not recorded" and "Unknown" are non-response. "N/A" cannot be assumed to mean code 8 ("not applicable"): comparing ages shows that code 8 is only used for children aged 0–4, while the placeholders occur at ages up to 72:

```{r}
#| label: Attendance Codes Placeholder Verification

attendance_text <- c("N/A", "not recorded", "Unknown")
D02 |>
  filter(education_attendance_code %in% c("8", attendance_text)) |>
  group_by(value = education_attendance_code) |>
  summarise(rows = n(), min_age = min(age), median_age = median(age), max_age = max(age))
```

**Treatment:** set the text placeholders to missing, record why in `education_attendance_flag`, and convert the column to integer.

```{r}
#| label: Fixing Broken Attendance Codes

D02 <- D02 |>
  mutate(
    education_attendance_flag = if_else(education_attendance_code %in% attendance_text, paste0("text placeholder '", education_attendance_code, "' set to missing"), NA_character_),
    
    education_attendance_code = as.integer(if_else(education_attendance_code %in% attendance_text, NA_character_, education_attendance_code))
  )

```

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Fixed Attendance Codes

D02 |> count(education_attendance_code, education_attendance_flag)
class(D02$education_attendance_code)
```

**Effect:** `education_attendance_code` is now an integer column holding only dictionary codes (1, 2, 3, 8) or missing. The `r sum(!is.na(D02$education_attendance_flag))` former placeholders are traceable through the flag. Code 3 ("do not know") is handled in section 4 with the other special codes.

## 2.4 Repairs from other datasets

### Age (D01)

**Problem:** the data dictionary gives a valid age range of 0–110. D01 has `r sum(is.na(D01$age))` missing ages and `r sum(D01$age < 0 | D01$age > 110, na.rm = TRUE)` ages outside that range. D02 and D03 record the age of the same people.

**Investigation:** check that D02 and D03 agree with each other, and that D01 agrees with D03 wherever D01's age is valid:

```{r}
#| label: Ages Inspection

age_check <- D01 |>
  left_join(select(D03, household_id, person_number, age_d03 = age), by = c("household_id", "person_number")) |>
  left_join(select(D02, household_id, person_number, age_d02 = age), by = c("household_id", "person_number"))

age_check |>
  summarise(
    
    rows = n(),
    
    d02_vs_d03_mismatches = sum(age_d02 != age_d03),
    
    d03_ages_outside_0_110 = sum(age_d03 < 0 | age_d03 > 110),
    
    d01_valid_ages_agreeing_with_d03 = sum(age == age_d03 & between(age, 0, 110), na.rm = TRUE),
    
    d01_valid_ages_disagreeing_with_d03 = sum(age != age_d03 & between(age, 0, 110), na.rm = TRUE),
    
    d01_missing = sum(is.na(age)),
    
    d01_invalid = sum(age < 0 | age > 110, na.rm = TRUE)
    
  )

age_check |>
  filter(age < 0 | age > 110) |> select(household_id, person_number, age_d01 = age, age_d02, age_d03)
```

D02 and D03 agree on every person and contain no invalid ages, and D01 agrees with them on every valid age. The only disagreements are D01's invalid values, so D03's age is a reliable replacement. Deleting these people would lose valid education and employment records for no reason.

**Treatment:** replace D01's missing and invalid ages with D03's age and record which rows changed in `age_flag`.

```{r}
#| label: Fixed Ages

D01 <- age_check |>
  mutate(
    
    age_flag = case_when(is.na(age) ~ "missing - filled from D03",
      age < 0 | age > 110 ~ paste0("invalid (", age, ") - replaced from D03")
    ),
    
    age = if_else(is.na(age) | age < 0 | age > 110, age_d03, age)
  ) |>
  
  select(-age_d02, -age_d03)
```

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Verification of Ages after Fix

tibble(
  rows = nrow(D01),
  
  missing_age = sum(is.na(D01$age)),
  
  min_age = min(D01$age),
  
  max_age = max(D01$age),
  
  ages_differing_from_d03 = sum(D01$age != age_check$age_d03)
)

D01 |> count(age_flag = if_else(is.na(age_flag), "unchanged", str_remove(age_flag, " \\(.*\\)")))
```

**Effect:** `r sum(!is.na(D01$age_flag))` ages are repaired and none are deleted. D01's age now lies between 0 and 110 with no missing values, and agrees with D02 and D03 for every person.

### Education level (D02)

**Problem:** `education_level_code` in D02 has `r sum(is.na(D02$education_level_code))` missing values. D03 records the same variable for the same people.

```{r}
#| label: Education Dataset Inspection

D02_education_missing_before <- sum(is.na(D02$education_level_code)) #Kept for the before/after check below

education_check <- D02 |>
  left_join(select(D03, household_id, person_number, education_d03 = education_level_code), by = c("household_id", "person_number"))

education_check |>
  summarise(
    
    rows = n(),
    
    missing_in_d02 = sum(is.na(education_level_code)),
    
    missing_in_d03 = sum(is.na(education_d03)),
    
    agree_where_both_present = sum(education_level_code == education_d03, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    disagree_where_both_present = sum(education_level_code != education_d03, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    d02_missing_but_d03_present = sum(is.na(education_level_code) & !is.na(education_d03))
    
  )
```

**Treatment:** D02 and D03 never disagree, and D03 has no missing values, so D02's gaps are filled from D03 and flagged in `education_level_flag`.

```{r}
#| label: Fixed Education Dataset 

D02 <- education_check |>
  mutate(
    education_level_flag = if_else(is.na(education_level_code), "missing - filled from D03", NA_character_),
    education_level_code = coalesce(education_level_code, education_d03)
  ) |>
  select(-education_d03)

tibble(

       missing_before = D02_education_missing_before,
       
       missing_after = sum(is.na(D02$education_level_code)),
       
       rows_flagged = sum(!is.na(D02$education_level_flag))
)
```

**Effect:** D02's education level is complete. Code 99, which appears in both D02 and D03 but not in the dictionary, is not a gap and cannot be filled from D03. It is treated with the other special codes in section 4.

```{r}
)
```

Columns dropped from each dataset:

```{r}
#| label: Columns Dropped

#Dropped columns for each dataset, stacked into one table
columns_dropped <- bind_rows(
  tibble(dataset = "D01", column = setdiff(D01_columns_before, names(D01))),
  tibble(dataset = "D02", column = setdiff(D02_columns_before, names(D02))),
  tibble(dataset = "D03", column = setdiff(D03_columns_before, names(D03))),
  tibble(dataset = "D08", column = setdiff(D08_columns_before, names(D08)))
) |>
  
  #Detailed Table explainning why each column gets dropped
  mutate(
    reason = case_when(
    column == "survey_year" ~ "No information (always 2024)",
    
    column == "province" ~ "Messy text, rebuilt from province_code",
    
    column %in% c("province_code", "age", "sex_code", "geo_type_code", "person_weight") ~ "Duplicate of D01",
    
    column == "education_level_code" ~ "Duplicate of D02 (used to fill D02's gaps in 2.4)",
    
    column %in% c("age_group_code", "employment_status1code", "grade_code") ~ "Duplicate of another column",
    
    column %in% c("wage_work_code", "business_work_code", "volunteer_work_code", "retired_code", "looking_for_work_code", "could_start_work_code", "transport_to_work_code", "minutes_to_work", "sector_code", "work_internet_code", "study_internet_code") ~ "Leakage: reveals or defines an outcome",
    
    column %in% c("language_code", "relationship_to_head_code", "marital_status_code") ~ "Not needed for any hypothesis",
    
    column == "metro_code" ~ "Too detailed (disclosure risk)",
    
    column %in% c("public_private_institution_code", "transport_mode_to_education_code", "travel_time_to_education", "bursary_code", "total_education_fees", "no_fees_school_code", "school_food_programme_code", "absence_code", "absence_days") ~ "Only recorded for people already attending",
    
    column == "salary_amount_raw" ~ "Unusable (not Rand amounts)",
    
    column %in% c("salary_period_code", "salary_category_code") ~ "Salary detail not needed (lab_salary_raw kept)",
    
    column %in% c("telephone_code", "cellphone_code", "household_mobile_phones") ~ "Phones, not internet access",
    
    column %in% c("public_wi_fi_internet_code", "library_internet_code", "cafe_internet_code") ~ "Internet access outside the home",
    
    column == "household_weight" ~ "Household weight, not needed at person grain",
    
    TRUE ~ "NOT CLASSIFIED" #Should never appear; shows up if a dropped column has no reason
  )
  )

columns_dropped |>
  group_by(dataset, reason) |>
  summarise(columns_dropped = n(), columns = paste(column, collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop")
```

**Effect:** the four datasets go from `r sum(uncleaned_summary$cols)` uncleaned columns to `r ncol(D01) + ncol(D02) + ncol(D03) + ncol(D08)`, of which `r sum(str_ends(c(names(D01), names(D02), names(D03), names(D08)), "_flag"))` are the traceability flags from section 2. All `r nrow(columns_dropped)` dropped columns have a documented reason (`r sum(columns_dropped$reason == "NOT CLASSIFIED")` are "NOT CLASSIFIED"). `select()` removes columns only, so every person and household cleaned in section 2 is still present.

# 4. Special Values

Several kept columns contain values that are not ordinary answers: structural "not applicable" codes, non-response codes, codes missing from the data dictionary, and placeholder amounts in `lab_salary_raw`. Each is classified from evidence before anything is changed.

## 4.1 Special codes in the kept columns

**Problem:** the kept code columns mix valid categories with "not applicable" codes, non-response codes and codes that are not in the data dictionary. Treating them all as ordinary categories would put "do not know" next to real answers, while deleting the rows would lose the same people's other valid answers.

```{r}
#| label: Special Codes Check

D02 |> count(education_level_code, sort = TRUE) |> filter(education_level_code %in% c(98, 99, 29, 28))

D02 |> count(education_attendance_code)

D02 |> count(institution_type_code == 88, name = "rows")

D02 |> count(reason_not_attending_code == 88, name = "rows")

D08 |> count(fixed_internet_code)

D08 |> count(mobile_internet_code)

D08 |> count(computer_asset_code)
```

**Treatment:** classify each special code as a valid category, a "Not applicable" level or `NA`, as listed in the table below. The classification is applied in section 6 when the label columns are created: codes left out of `factor()`'s levels become `NA`.

- Codes 98 (No schooling) and 28 (Other) in `education_level_code` are real education levels and stay valid categories.
- Codes 29 and 3 mean "do not know", and `computer_asset_code` 9 means "Unspecified". These are non-response, not categories, so they become `NA`.
- Code 99 in `education_level_code` and code 9 in `fixed_internet_code` and `mobile_internet_code` are not in the data dictionary, so they cannot be given a meaning and become `NA`.
- Code 88 in `institution_type_code` and `reason_not_attending_code` means the question did not apply to the person (for example, a reason for not attending is only asked of people who do not attend). It becomes a "Not applicable" level, not missing.
- Attendance code 8 only occurs under age 15 and disappears after record selection (section 5).

```{r}
#| label: Special Code Classification

tibble(
  
  column = c("education_level_code", "education_level_code", "education_level_code", "education_level_code", "education_attendance_code", "education_attendance_code", "institution_type_code", "reason_not_attending_code", "fixed_internet_code", "mobile_internet_code", "computer_asset_code"),

  code = c(98, 28, 29, 99, 3, 8, 88, 88, 9, 9, 9),

  meaning = c("No schooling", "Other", "Do not know", "Not in the data dictionary", "Do not know", "Not applicable (only under age 15)", "Not applicable", "Not applicable", "Not in the data dictionary", "Not in the data dictionary", "Unspecified"),

  classification = c("Valid category", "Valid category", "NA (non-response)", "NA (undocumented code)", "NA (non-response)", "Removed by record selection", "'Not applicable' level", "'Not applicable' level", "NA (undocumented code)", "NA (undocumented code)", "NA (non-response)"),

  rows = c(sum(D02$education_level_code %in% 98), sum(D02$education_level_code %in% 28), sum(D02$education_level_code %in% 29), sum(D02$education_level_code %in% 99), sum(D02$education_attendance_code %in% 3), sum(D02$education_attendance_code %in% 8), sum(D02$institution_type_code %in% 88), sum(D02$reason_not_attending_code %in% 88), sum(D08$fixed_internet_code %in% 9), sum(D08$mobile_internet_code %in% 9), sum(D08$computer_asset_code %in% 9))
  
)
```

Two groups of values were already `NA` before this section. They stay `NA` because there is no dictionary code to assign them:

- The `r sum(is.na(D02$education_attendance_code))` missing values in `education_attendance_code` are not original gaps, because the uncleaned column had no missing values. They are the text placeholders ("N/A", "Unknown", "not recorded") set to missing and flagged in 2.3.
- The `r sum(is.na(D08$mobile_internet_code))` missing values in `mobile_internet_code` were already missing in the uncleaned data.

**Effect / Verification:** no values are changed in this section, and every `_code` column keeps its original codes. The classification takes effect in section 6. The "Codes Without a Label" table there verifies it: the rows left without a label are exactly the rows holding the codes classified as `NA` here, after record selection.

## 4.2 Salary placeholders

**Problem:** `lab_salary_raw` mixes real Rand values with two placeholder codes, 888888888 and 999999999. Left in place, they would be read as salaries of almost R1 billion. Their meaning also has to be checked against employment status before deciding how to treat them.

```{r}
#| label: Salary Placeholder Cross-Tab

D03 |>
  mutate(salary_type = case_when(
    lab_salary_raw == 888888888 ~ "888888888 (don't know/refused)",
    lab_salary_raw == 999999999 ~ "999999999 (not applicable)",
    TRUE ~ "Real salary value"
  )) |>
  count(employment_status2code, salary_type) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = employment_status2code, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

```

**Treatment:** the cross-table shows that 888888888 acts as "not applicable" for everyone without a job, and 999999999 as non-response among the employed. Both placeholders become `NA` in a new `salary` column, and a new `salary_status` column records why a salary is missing. It is derived from the value and `employment_status2code` together, not from the placeholder alone. `lab_salary_raw` is kept unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: Salary Reversal

D03_salary_missing_before <- sum(D03$lab_salary_raw %in% c(888888888, 999999999))

D03 <- D03 |>
  mutate(
    salary = if_else(lab_salary_raw %in% c(888888888, 999999999), NA_real_, lab_salary_raw),
    salary_status = case_when(
!is.na(salary) ~ "Reported", lab_salary_raw == 999999999 ~ "Non-response (employed)", lab_salary_raw == 888888888 &
employment_status2code == 1 ~ "Non-response (employed)", lab_salary_raw == 888888888 ~ "Not applicable (not employed)", TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

```

**Effect:** `r format(sum(!is.na(D03$salary) & D03$employment_status2code == 1), big.mark = ",")` of `r format(sum(D03$employment_status2code == 1), big.mark = ",")` employed people report a real salary (`r round(mean(!is.na(D03$salary[D03$employment_status2code == 1])) * 100)`%). This corrects Milestone 1's "74% unusable" figure, which counted people who cannot have a salary in the first place.

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Salary Reversal Verification

D03 |> count(salary_status, has_salary = !is.na(salary))

tibble(
  
  placeholders_before = D03_salary_missing_before,
  placeholders_remaining_in_salary = sum(D03$salary %in% c(888888888, 999999999), na.rm = TRUE)
  
)
```

# 5. Record Selection (ages 15–64)

**Problem:** the analysis population is the working-age population, ages 15–64.

**Treatment:** filter D01 on `between(age, 15, 64)`, then keep only matching people in D02 and D03 with `semi_join()`. All D08 households are kept; Task 3 reports the households with no working-age member. The number of people in each household is counted before the filter, because the smartphone check in section 7 needs the full household size, not just the working-age members.

**Household composition (used in section 10):** the household features in section 10.3.5 need the number of children (under 15) and older people (65+) in each household. The age filter below removes these people, so every member of each household is counted first.

```{r}
#| label: Household Composition Before Record Selection

#Counts all members of each household before the 15-64 filter removes children and people aged 65+
household_composition <- D01 |>
  group_by(household_id) |>
  summarise(
    household_size = n(),
    n_children_under15 = sum(age < 15),
    n_elderly_65plus = sum(age > 64),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

tibble(
  households = nrow(household_composition),

  people_counted = sum(household_composition$household_size),

  people_in_D01 = nrow(D01),

  children_counted = sum(household_composition$n_children_under15),

  aged_65_plus_counted = sum(household_composition$n_elderly_65plus)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: Record Selection

D01_rows_before_selection <- nrow(D01)
D01_under_15 <- sum(D01$age < 15)
D01_65_plus <- sum(D01$age > 64)

#All members of each household, counted before the age filter (used in section 7)
household_size <- D01 |> count(household_id, name = "household_size")

D01 <- D01 |> filter(between(age, 15, 64))
D02 <- semi_join(D02, D01, by = c("household_id", "person_number"))
D03 <- semi_join(D03, D01, by = c("household_id", "person_number"))
```

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Record Selection Verification

tibble(
  
  dataset = c("D01", "D02", "D03"),
  
  rows_before = D01_rows_before_selection,
  
  rows_after = c(nrow(D01), nrow(D02), nrow(D03)),
  
  removed_under_15 = D01_under_15,
  
  removed_65_plus = D01_65_plus,
  
  distinct_households = c(n_distinct(D01$household_id), n_distinct(D02$household_id), n_distinct(D03$household_id)),
  
  identical_keys_to_D01 = c(TRUE, setequal(paste(D01$household_id, D01$person_number), paste(D02$household_id, D02$person_number)), setequal(paste(D01$household_id, D01$person_number), paste(D03$household_id, D03$person_number)))
  
)
```

**Effect:** all three person files have `r format(nrow(D01), big.mark = ",")` rows and identical keys, covering `r format(n_distinct(D01$household_id), big.mark = ",")` households. `r format(D01_under_15, big.mark = ",")` people under 15 and `r format(D01_65_plus, big.mark = ",")` aged 65+ were removed.

# 6. Data Transformation: recoding into labelled factors

**Problem:** `_code` columns are not analytically meaningful or safe to treat as numbers. A model would treat province 9 as "more" than province 1, and a report reader cannot tell what code 5 means without the data dictionary.

**Treatment:** for every kept `_code` column, add a label column of the same name without the suffix, using `factor(..., levels =, labels =)` with the labels from the data dictionary. Codes left out of `levels =` become `NA`, applying the classification from section 4. `_code` columns are never modified, so every label can be traced back to its original code.

```{r}
#| label: Recode D01

D01 <- D01 |>
  mutate(
    province = factor(province_code, levels = 1:9, labels = c("Western Cape", "Eastern Cape", "Northern Cape", "Free State", "KwaZulu-Natal", "North West", "Gauteng", "Mpumalanga", "Limpopo")),
    
    sex = factor(sex_code, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    
    population_group = factor(population_group_code, levels = 1:4, labels = c("Black African", "Coloured", "Indian/Asian", "White")),
    
    geo_type = factor(geo_type_code, levels = 1:3, labels = c("Urban", "Traditional", "Farms")),
    
    metro = factor(metro_indicator, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Metro", "Non-metro"))
    
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: Recode D02

D02 <- D02 |>
  mutate(
    education_level =
      factor(education_level_code, levels = c(98, 0:27, 28),
         labels = c(
             "No schooling",
             "Grade R/0", "Grade 1/Sub A/Class 1", "Grade 2/Sub B/Class 2",
             "Grade 3/Standard 1/ABET/AET 1", "Grade 4/Standard 2",

  )
```

```{r}
#| label: Recode D08

D08 <- D08 |>

    fixed_internet = factor(fixed_internet_code, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Yes", "No")),
```

**Verification:** every code maps to exactly one label, and only the codes classified as non-response in section 4 have no label.

```{r}
#| label: Recode Verification

D01 |> count(province_code, province)
D01 |> count(sex_code, sex)
D01 |> count(population_group_code, population_group)
D01 |> count(geo_type_code, geo_type)

D02 |> count(education_level_code, education_level)
D02 |> count(education_attendance_code, education_attendance)

D02 |> count(reason_not_attending_code, reason_not_attending)
```
