```{r}
D08 |> count(fixed_internet_code, fixed_internet)
D08 |> count(mobile_internet_code, mobile_internet)
D08 |> count(computer_asset_code, computer_asset)
```

```{r}
#| label: Codes Without a Label

#Rows with a code but no label, compared with the number of rows holding the non-response codes from section 4
tibble(
  
  label_column = c("education_level", "education_attendance", "fixed_internet", "mobile_internet", "computer_asset"),

  codes_set_to_NA = c("29, 99", "3", "9", "9", "9"),

  rows_with_these_codes = 
    c(sum(D02$education_level_code %in% c(29, 99)), sum(D02$education_attendance_code %in% 3), sum(D08$fixed_internet_code %in% 9), sum(D08$mobile_internet_code %in% 9), sum(D08$computer_asset_code %in% 9)),

  rows_with_code_but_no_label = 
    c(sum(!is.na(D02$education_level_code) & is.na(D02$education_level)), sum(!is.na(D02$education_attendance_code) & is.na(D02$education_attendance)), sum(!is.na(D08$fixed_internet_code) & is.na(D08$fixed_internet)), sum(!is.na(D08$mobile_internet_code) & is.na(D08$mobile_internet)), sum(!is.na(D08$computer_asset_code) & is.na(D08$computer_asset)))
  
)
```

**Effect:** 13 label columns are added (5 in D01, 4 in D02, 1 in D03 and 3 in D08) and no `_code` column is changed. The two columns in the table above always match, so the only codes left without a label are the non-response and undocumented codes classified in section 4: `r sum(D02$education_level_code %in% c(29, 99))` education levels, `r sum(D02$education_attendance_code %in% 3)` attendance values, `r sum(D08$fixed_internet_code %in% 9)` fixed internet, `r sum(D08$mobile_internet_code %in% 9)` mobile internet and `r sum(D08$computer_asset_code %in% 9)` computer asset values. `institution_type` and `reason_not_attending` now use the data dictionary's descriptions, and code 88 is kept as "Not applicable" rather than missing.

The levels of `education_level` follow the dictionary order, which is not a ranking: "No schooling" comes first and "Other" comes last. Education bands built for the analysis in Task 3 must therefore group explicit codes, not rely on the level order.

# 7. Outlier Review

`age`, `household_smartphones` and `salary` are the only kept columns that are real measurements rather than categories, so they are the only columns checked for outliers and impossible values. Each is shown as a histogram and a boxplot. The boxplot's whiskers end at the fences, 1.5 × the interquartile range (IQR) beyond the quartiles, and points outside the fences are drawn separately as statistical outliers. A statistical outlier is only a candidate: it is kept unless domain evidence shows the value is impossible.

## 7.1 Age

**Problem:** extreme ages could distort any analysis by age.

```{r}
#| label: Age Outlier Check

summary(D01$age)

ggplot(D01, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Age distribution after record selection", x = "Age", y = "Count")

ggplot(D01, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Age after record selection (boxplot)", x = "Age", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())

#Boxplot fences: 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles
age_boxplot <- tibble(

  q1 = quantile(D01$age, 0.25),

  median = median(D01$age),

  q3 = quantile(D01$age, 0.75),

  lower_fence = q1 - 1.5 * (q3 - q1),

  upper_fence = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1),

  points_below_fence = sum(D01$age < lower_fence),

  points_above_fence = sum(D01$age > upper_fence)
)

age_boxplot
```

**Treatment:** none. Invalid ages were already repaired in 2.4, and record selection (section 5) limits age to 15–64.

**Effect / Verification:** the summary shows a minimum of `r min(D01$age)` and a maximum of `r max(D01$age)`. The histogram shows no isolated values, and the boxplot has `r age_boxplot$points_below_fence + age_boxplot$points_above_fence` points outside its fences (`r age_boxplot$lower_fence` to `r age_boxplot$upper_fence`), so there are no age outliers left to treat.

## 7.2 Household smartphones

**Problem:** a household cannot own a negative number of smartphones, but D08 contains `r sum(D08$household_smartphones < 0, na.rm = TRUE)` negative counts. Very high counts also need to be checked against the size of the household.

```{r}
#| label: Smartphones Outlier Check

summary(D08$household_smartphones)

ggplot(D08, aes(x = household_smartphones)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Household smartphones before treatment (boxplot)", x = "Smartphones in the household", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())

#Boxplot fences: 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles
smartphones_boxplot <- tibble(

  q1 = quantile(D08$household_smartphones, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),

  median = median(D08$household_smartphones, na.rm = TRUE),

  q3 = quantile(D08$household_smartphones, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),

  lower_fence = q1 - 1.5 * (q3 - q1),

  upper_fence = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1),

  points_below_fence = sum(D08$household_smartphones < lower_fence, na.rm = TRUE),

  points_above_fence = sum(D08$household_smartphones > upper_fence, na.rm = TRUE)
)

smartphones_boxplot

D08 |> filter(household_smartphones < 0) |> count(household_smartphones)

D08 |>
  left_join(household_size, by = "household_id") |>
  filter(household_smartphones >= 10) |>
  select(household_id, household_smartphones, household_size)
```

In the boxplot, the `r smartphones_boxplot$points_below_fence` points below the lower fence are exactly the negative counts. Most households have 1 or 2 smartphones, so the box is narrow (an IQR of `r smartphones_boxplot$q3 - smartphones_boxplot$q1`). As a result, the 1.5 × IQR rule also marks every household with `r floor(smartphones_boxplot$upper_fence) + 1` or more smartphones as an outlier: `r format(smartphones_boxplot$points_above_fence, big.mark = ",")` households. These high points are a result of the narrow box, not evidence of errors, so they are checked against household size instead of being removed.

The negative values cannot be repaired: no other kept dataset records smartphones, and removing the minus sign is not justified, because `r sum(D08$household_smartphones < -13, na.rm = TRUE)` of them would then exceed the dictionary maximum of 13. At the other end, every household with 10 or more smartphones has at least as many members as smartphones. `household_size` counts all members, including those outside the 15–64 range, because it was counted before record selection (section 5).

**Treatment:** set the negative counts to `NA` and record the original value in `household_smartphones_flag`. The high counts are plausible and kept unchanged. The household is kept, since its other connectivity columns are still valid.

```{r}
#| label: Fixing Negative Smartphone Counts

D08_negative_smartphones_before <- sum(D08$household_smartphones < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

D08 <- D08 |>
  mutate(
    
    household_smartphones_flag = if_else(household_smartphones < 0, paste0("invalid negative count (", household_smartphones, ") set to missing"), NA_character_),
    
    household_smartphones = if_else(household_smartphones < 0, NA_real_, household_smartphones)
    
  )

```

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Smartphones Verification

D08 |>
  left_join(household_size, by = "household_id") |>
  summarise(
    
    negative_before = D08_negative_smartphones_before,

    negative_after = sum(household_smartphones < 0, na.rm = TRUE),

    missing_after = sum(is.na(household_smartphones)),

    rows_flagged = sum(!is.na(household_smartphones_flag)),

    min_after = min(household_smartphones, na.rm = TRUE),

    max_after = max(household_smartphones, na.rm = TRUE),

    households_with_more_smartphones_than_members = sum(household_smartphones > household_size, na.rm = TRUE)

  )

ggplot(D08, aes(x = household_smartphones)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Household smartphones after treatment (boxplot)", x = "Smartphones in the household", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

**Effect:** the `r D08_negative_smartphones_before` impossible counts are now `NA` and traceable through `household_smartphones_flag`, and no household is removed. After treatment, the boxplot has no points below the box. The remaining counts lie within the dictionary range of 0–13, and no household has more smartphones than members, including the `r format(smartphones_boxplot$points_above_fence, big.mark = ",")` households above the upper fence, which are kept unchanged. `household_size` is not joined onto D08 or saved; it is only used for this check.

## 7.3 Salary

**Problem:** reported salaries range from very small to very large values, and a few extreme values could distort averages.

```{r}
#| label: Salary Outlier Check

D03 |> filter(!is.na(salary)) |> summarise(
  min = min(salary), p1 = quantile(salary, 0.01), median = median(salary),
  p99 = quantile(salary, 0.99), max = max(salary)
)

D03 |>
  filter(!is.na(salary)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = salary)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Reported salary (log scale)", x = "Salary (Rand, log scale)", y = "Count")

#Drawn on the log scale like the histogram; on the Rand scale the box is squashed against zero
D03 |>
  filter(!is.na(salary)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = salary)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Reported salary (boxplot, log scale)", subtitle = "Dashed line: R100 threshold used for salary_flag",
       x = "Salary (Rand, log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())

#Boxplot fences on the log scale, converted back to Rand
salary_boxplot <- D03 |>
  filter(!is.na(salary)) |>
  summarise(

    log_q1 = quantile(log10(salary), 0.25),

    log_q3 = quantile(log10(salary), 0.75),

    lower_fence_rand = 10^(log_q1 - 1.5 * (log_q3 - log_q1)),

    upper_fence_rand = 10^(log_q3 + 1.5 * (log_q3 - log_q1)),

    points_below_fence = sum(salary < lower_fence_rand),

    points_above_fence = sum(salary > upper_fence_rand),

    of_which_under_R100 = sum(salary < 100)
  ) |>
  select(-log_q1, -log_q3)

salary_boxplot
```

On the log scale, the boxplot marks `r salary_boxplot$points_below_fence` salaries below about R`r format(round(salary_boxplot$lower_fence_rand), big.mark = ",")` and `r salary_boxplot$points_above_fence` above about R`r format(round(salary_boxplot$upper_fence_rand), big.mark = ",")` as outliers.

**Treatment:** the high outliers, up to R`r format(max(D03$salary, na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ",")`, are genuine high earners and are kept. The low outliers are not all errors: values between R100 and about R`r format(round(salary_boxplot$lower_fence_rand), big.mark = ",")` are low but possible for casual or part-time work, and are kept unflagged. Only the `r salary_boxplot$of_which_under_R100` values under R100 cannot plausibly be a monthly salary. They are flagged in `salary_flag`, not deleted, since the pay period is not documented in the source data. The flag uses the fixed R100 threshold, not the boxplot fence, so it does not depend on the rest of the data.

```{r}
#| label: Flagging Low Salary Outliers

D03 <- D03 |>
  mutate(salary_flag = if_else(!is.na(salary) & salary < 100, "Implausibly low for a monthly salary", NA_character_))
```

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Salary Flag Verification

D03 |>
  filter(!is.na(salary)) |>
  summarise(
    reported_salaries = n(),
    
    flagged_under_R100 = sum(!is.na(salary_flag)),
    
    largest_flagged_salary = max(salary[!is.na(salary_flag)]),
    
    smallest_unflagged_salary = min(salary[is.na(salary_flag)])
)

```

**Effect:** `r sum(!is.na(D03$salary_flag))` of `r format(sum(!is.na(D03$salary)), big.mark = ",")` reported salaries are flagged and every salary value is unchanged. Because the threshold is fixed, later analyses can include or exclude these rows with `salary < 100`, even without the flag column.

`person_weight` is not touched: survey weights must never be trimmed or scaled. No scaling or transformation is applied during preprocessing; that belongs in Task 4, after the train/test split, to avoid leakage. The log scale above is for plotting only.

# 8. Validation and Save of the Cleaned Datasets

## 8.1 Validation of the cleaned datasets

**Problem:** the cleaned datasets will be used in every later task, so before saving them it must be shown that the pipeline as a whole did what the earlier sections claim. People must only have been removed by record selection, keys must still be unique, no duplicates may remain, and every remaining missing value must have a reason. The rubric also requires before-and-after evidence for every major preprocessing decision.

**Treatment:** compare each cleaned dataset with the uncleaned summary recorded in 1.2, list the columns added or changed in type, and give a reason for every column that still has missing values.

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Before vs After Preprocessing

tibble(
  
  dataset = c("D01", "D02", "D03", "D08"),
  
  rows_uncleaned = uncleaned_summary$rows,
  
  rows_cleaned = c(nrow(D01), nrow(D02), nrow(D03), nrow(D08)),
  
  cols_uncleaned = uncleaned_summary$cols,
  
  cols_cleaned = c(ncol(D01), ncol(D02), ncol(D03), ncol(D08)),
  
  missing_values_uncleaned = uncleaned_summary$missing_values,
  
  #_flag columns are left out: they are empty by design for every row that was not changed
  missing_values_cleaned = c(sum(is.na(select(D01, -ends_with("_flag")))), sum(is.na(select(D02, -ends_with("_flag")))), sum(is.na(select(D03, -ends_with("_flag")))), sum(is.na(select(D08, -ends_with("_flag"))))),
  
  distinct_keys_uncleaned = uncleaned_summary$distinct_keys,
  
  distinct_keys_cleaned = c(nrow(distinct(D01, household_id, person_number)), nrow(distinct(D02, household_id, person_number)), nrow(distinct(D03, household_id, person_number)),
                            
  n_distinct(D08$household_id)),
  
  exact_duplicates_uncleaned = uncleaned_summary$exact_duplicate_rows,
  
  exact_duplicates_cleaned = c(nrow(D01) - nrow(distinct(D01)), nrow(D02) - nrow(distinct(D02)), nrow(D03) - nrow(distinct(D03)), nrow(D08) - nrow(distinct(D08)))
  
)
```

**Note:** `missing_values_cleaned` leaves out the `_flag` columns, which are empty by design for every row that was not changed. D01 has no missing values left. The cleaned counts for D02, D03 and D08 are higher than the uncleaned ones, but this is not new data loss: placeholders, non-response codes and impossible values were stored as ordinary values in the uncleaned data, so the uncleaned count did not see them. They are now honest `NA`s. In D03, `salary` is `NA` for the placeholders reversed in 4.2, and nearly all of these belong to people who are not employed and cannot have a salary. In D02 and D08 the extra `NA`s come from the text placeholders set to missing in 2.3, the negative smartphone counts in 7.2, and the label columns from section 6, which repeat the missing values of their `_code` column and leave the non-response codes without a label. The Final Missingness table below gives the reason for every column.

Columns added or changed in type since column selection (section 3):

```{r}
#| label: Types Before and After Sections 4 to 7

bind_rows(
  D01 = enframe(D01_types_before, name = "column", value = "type_before") |>
    full_join(enframe(sapply(D01, class), name = "column", value = "type_after"), by = "column"),
  
  D02 = enframe(D02_types_before, name = "column", value = "type_before") |>
    full_join(enframe(sapply(D02, class), name = "column", value = "type_after"), by = "column"),
  
  D03 = enframe(D03_types_before, name = "column", value = "type_before") |>
    full_join(enframe(sapply(D03, class), name = "column", value = "type_after"), by = "column"),
  
  D08 = enframe(D08_types_before, name = "column", value = "type_before") |>
    full_join(enframe(sapply(D08, class), name = "column", value = "type_after"), by = "column"),
  .id = "dataset"
) |>
  filter(is.na(type_before) != is.na(type_after) | (!is.na(type_before) & !is.na(type_after) & type_before != type_after))
```

```{r}
#| label: Final Missingness

final_missingness <- bind_rows(
  D01 = enframe(colSums(is.na(D01)), name = "column", value = "missing"),
  D02 = enframe(colSums(is.na(D02)), name = "column", value = "missing"),
  D03 = enframe(colSums(is.na(D03)), name = "column", value = "missing"),
  D08 = enframe(colSums(is.na(D08)), name = "column", value = "missing"),
  .id = "dataset"
) |>
  filter(missing > 0) |>
  mutate(
    reason = case_when(
    column == "education_level" ~ "Codes 29/99 reclassified to NA in sections 4/6",
    
    column == "education_attendance_code" ~ "Text placeholders ('N/A', 'Unknown', 'not recorded') set to NA and flagged in 2.3",
    
    column == "education_attendance" ~ "Code 3 reclassified to NA in sections 4/6, plus the text placeholders set to NA in 2.3",
    
    column == "fixed_internet" ~ "Code 9 reclassified to NA in sections 4/6",
    
    column == "mobile_internet_code" ~ "Already missing in the uncleaned data; no dictionary code to assign (noted in section 4)",
    
    column == "mobile_internet" ~ "Code 9 reclassified to NA in sections 4/6, plus the missing mobile_internet_code values",
    
    column == "computer_asset" ~ "Code 9 ('Unspecified') reclassified to NA in sections 4/6",
    
    column == "household_smartphones" ~ "Negative counts set to NA and flagged in 7.2",
    
    str_detect(column, "_flag$") ~ "Flags only filled in for rows that changed (expected)",
    
    column == "salary" ~ "Placeholder codes reversed to NA in section 4",
    
    column == "salary_status" ~ "Could not be classified from value and employment status",
    
    TRUE ~ "NOT CLASSIFIED"
  ))

final_missingness
```

```{r}
#| label: Final Category Levels

list(
  
  province = levels(D01$province), sex = levels(D01$sex), population_group = levels(D01$population_group),
  
  geo_type = levels(D01$geo_type), metro = levels(D01$metro),
  
  education_level = levels(D02$education_level), education_attendance = levels(D02$education_attendance),
  
  institution_type = levels(D02$institution_type), reason_not_attending = levels(D02$reason_not_attending),
  
  employment_status = levels(D03$employment_status),
  
  fixed_internet = levels(D08$fixed_internet), mobile_internet = levels(D08$mobile_internet),
  
  computer_asset = levels(D08$computer_asset)
)
```

**Effect:** D01 goes from `r format(uncleaned_summary$rows[1], big.mark = ",")` to `r format(nrow(D01), big.mark = ",")` people. The difference is exactly the `r format(D01_under_15 + D01_65_plus, big.mark = ",")` people outside ages 15–64 removed in section 5, so no one was lost to cleaning. D02 and D03 match D01 after also losing their `r D02_exact_duplicates` and `r D03_exact_duplicates` exact duplicate rows (2.2), and D08 keeps all `r format(nrow(D08), big.mark = ",")` households. In every dataset each key appears exactly once and no exact duplicates remain. `r sum(final_missingness$reason == "NOT CLASSIFIED")` of the `r nrow(final_missingness)` columns with missing values lack a documented reason.

## 8.2 Save

**Problem:** the cleaned datasets must be saved so that later tasks can use them without rerunning this pipeline. The original files in `Datasets/` must not be changed.

**Treatment:** save each cleaned dataset as a new `.csv` (required deliverable) in `Datasets/Cleaned/`. The original files are only read, never written. Missing values are written as empty cells rather than the text "NA", so that Power BI reads them as blanks instead of turning numeric columns such as `salary` into text. A CSV does not store column types or the order of factor levels. Anyone reading the CSVs, including Power BI, must therefore read `household_id` and `person_number` as text, and re-apply the level order listed above where the order matters.

The `_flag` columns are left out of the saved files. Inside this pipeline they stay in the datasets, so every change remains traceable in the report and in the integration steps (section 9). They are removed from the analytical data in Task 4, because they are not predictors. The saved files contain only the analytical columns: the original codes, the cleaned values and the labels.

Saving at this point, before the train/test split in Task 4, does not leak information between the future training and test rows. Every change so far either applies a fixed rule to each row (dictionary codes, the 15–64 age range, the R100 salary threshold, negative counts) or copies a value from the same person's record in another dataset. Nothing is estimated from the data as a whole: no means, quantiles, imputation models or scaling are used to change a value. Steps that learn from the data belong after the split, where they are fitted on the training rows only.

```{r}
#| label: Save Cleaned Datasets

#na = "" writes missing values as empty cells, which both R and Power BI read as missing
#select(-ends_with("_flag")) leaves the traceability flags out of the saved files; they stay in the datasets in memory
write_csv(select(D01, -ends_with("_flag")), file.path(cleaned_directory, "D01_clean.csv"), na = "")

write_csv(select(D02, -ends_with("_flag")), file.path(cleaned_directory, "D02_clean.csv"), na = "")

write_csv(select(D03, -ends_with("_flag")), file.path(cleaned_directory, "D03_clean.csv"), na = "")

write_csv(select(D08, -ends_with("_flag")), file.path(cleaned_directory, "D08_clean.csv"), na = "")
```

**Verification:** read the saved files back with the IDs as text, the same way later tasks should read them. Compare them with the datasets in memory without their flag columns, and confirm that no flag column was saved.

```{r}
#| label: Saved Files Verification

D01_saved <- read_csv(file.path(cleaned_directory, "D01_clean.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(household_id = col_character(), person_number = col_character()))

D02_saved <- read_csv(file.path(cleaned_directory, "D02_clean.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(household_id = col_character(), person_number = col_character()))

D03_saved <- read_csv(file.path(cleaned_directory, "D03_clean.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(household_id = col_character(), person_number = col_character()))

D08_saved <- read_csv(file.path(cleaned_directory, "D08_clean.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = cols(household_id = col_character()))

tibble(
  
  dataset = c("D01", "D02", "D03", "D08"),

  rows_in_memory = c(nrow(D01), nrow(D02), nrow(D03), nrow(D08)),

  rows_in_saved_file = c(nrow(D01_saved), nrow(D02_saved), nrow(D03_saved), nrow(D08_saved)),

  flag_columns_in_saved_file = c(sum(str_ends(names(D01_saved), "_flag")), sum(str_ends(names(D02_saved), "_flag")),
                                 sum(str_ends(names(D03_saved), "_flag")), sum(str_ends(names(D08_saved), "_flag"))),

  same_columns_apart_from_flags = c(identical(names(D01_saved), names(select(D01, -ends_with("_flag")))),
                                    identical(names(D02_saved), names(select(D02, -ends_with("_flag")))),
                                    identical(names(D03_saved), names(select(D03, -ends_with("_flag")))),
                                    identical(names(D08_saved), names(select(D08, -ends_with("_flag"))))),

  ids_identical = c(identical(D01_saved$household_id, D01$household_id) & identical(D01_saved$person_number, D01$person_number), identical(D02_saved$household_id, D02$household_id) & identical(D02_saved$person_number, D02$person_number), identical(D03_saved$household_id, D03$household_id) & identical(D03_saved$person_number, D03$person_number), identical(D08_saved$household_id, D08$household_id)),

  missing_values_identical = c(sum(is.na(D01_saved)) == sum(is.na(select(D01, -ends_with("_flag")))),
                               sum(is.na(D02_saved)) == sum(is.na(select(D02, -ends_with("_flag")))),
                               sum(is.na(D03_saved)) == sum(is.na(select(D03, -ends_with("_flag")))),
                               sum(is.na(D08_saved)) == sum(is.na(select(D08, -ends_with("_flag")))))

)
```

**Effect:** four new files are written to `Datasets/Cleaned/`. These four `write_csv()` calls are the only place the pipeline writes data, so the original files in `Datasets/` are left unchanged. Read back with the IDs as text, no saved file contains a flag column. Apart from the flags, every saved file has the same rows, columns, IDs and missing values as the cleaned dataset in memory, so later tasks can start from these files instead of rerunning the pipeline.

# 9. Data Integration

The analytical grain chosen in the Task 1 write-up is one row per working-age person (15–64), identified by `household_id` + `person_number`. Section 1.4 explains why only D01, D02, D03 and D08 are used. They are joined here, after cleaning, because the keys are only reliable once the missing IDs are recovered (2.1) and the duplicates removed (2.2), and the population is only final after record selection (section 5). D01 is the base table, because it now defines exactly this population. This section confirms the key and cardinality of each join before it runs, and verifies the row counts and unmatched records before and after every join.

## 9.1 Keys and cardinality before joining

**Problem:** a join duplicates rows if the key is not unique on the side that should match only once, and it silently drops or misaligns people if keys are missing or do not match. The expected cardinality of every join must be confirmed before the join is run.

```{r}
#| label: Key Checks Before Joining

tibble(

  dataset = c("D01", "D02", "D03", "D08"),

  key = c("household_id + person_number", "household_id + person_number", "household_id + person_number", "household_id"),

  rows = c(nrow(D01), nrow(D02), nrow(D03), nrow(D08)),

  distinct_keys = c(nrow(distinct(D01, household_id, person_number)), nrow(distinct(D02, household_id, person_number)),
                    nrow(distinct(D03, household_id, person_number)), n_distinct(D08$household_id)),

  missing_keys = c(sum(is.na(D01$household_id) | is.na(D01$person_number)), sum(is.na(D02$household_id) | is.na(D02$person_number)),
                   sum(is.na(D03$household_id) | is.na(D03$person_number)), sum(is.na(D08$household_id))),

  all_ids_18_digits = c(all(nchar(D01$household_id) == 18), all(nchar(D02$household_id) == 18),
                        all(nchar(D03$household_id) == 18), all(nchar(D08$household_id) == 18))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: Expected Cardinality and Unmatched Keys

#Households in D08 with no working-age member, and whether they had members before record selection (section 5)
D08_households_without_D01 <- anti_join(D08, D01, by = "household_id")

tibble(

  join = c("D01 + D02", "D01 + D03", "D01 + D08"),

  expected_cardinality = c("one-to-one", "one-to-one", "many-to-one"),

  most_D01_rows_per_key = c(max(count(D01, household_id, person_number)$n), max(count(D01, household_id, person_number)$n),
                            max(count(D01, household_id)$n)),

  most_rows_per_key_in_joined_dataset = c(max(count(D02, household_id, person_number)$n), max(count(D03, household_id, person_number)$n),
                                          max(count(D08, household_id)$n)),

  D01_rows_without_a_match = c(nrow(anti_join(D01, D02, by = c("household_id", "person_number"))),
                               nrow(anti_join(D01, D03, by = c("household_id", "person_number"))),
                               nrow(anti_join(D01, D08, by = "household_id"))),

  joined_dataset_rows_without_a_match = c(nrow(anti_join(D02, D01, by = c("household_id", "person_number"))),
                                          nrow(anti_join(D03, D01, by = c("household_id", "person_number"))),
                                          nrow(D08_households_without_D01))
)

tibble(
  D08_households_without_a_working_age_member = nrow(D08_households_without_D01),

  of_which_had_members_before_record_selection = sum(D08_households_without_D01$household_id %in% household_size$household_id)
)
```

**Treatment:** D01 is the left table, so every working-age person is kept. D02 and D03 are joined one-to-one on `household_id` + `person_number`. D08 is joined many-to-one on `household_id`, so each person receives their own household's connectivity values. Each join states its expected cardinality in dplyr's `relationship` argument, which stops the pipeline with an error if any key matches more rows than expected. The D02 and D03 joins also use `unmatched = "error"`, which stops the pipeline if any of their rows would be dropped. D08 cannot use `unmatched = "error"`, because its unmatched households are expected (see below).

**Effect / Verification:** every key is unique, complete and 18 digits long, and D01, D02 and D03 contain exactly the same people. Every person has a D08 household record, and each household appears once in D08, so no person can be duplicated. The only unmatched records are the `r format(nrow(D08_households_without_D01), big.mark = ",")` D08 households with no working-age member. All of them had members in D01 before record selection, so every one of their members is under 15 or over 64. They are outside the analysis population by design, not because of a key problem, and they remain available in `D08_clean.csv` for household-level description.

## 9.2 Joins

**Problem:** the brief requires row counts to be verified before and after each join, so the three joins are run one at a time.

**Treatment:** join D02, then D03, then D08 onto D01, recording the row count before each join.

```{r}
#| label: Join D01 and D02

integrated <- D01 |>
  left_join(D02, by = c("household_id", "person_number"), relationship = "one-to-one", unmatched = "error")

#education_level_code has no missing values in D02, so a missing value here would mean a person without a D02 match
tibble(
  join = "D01 + D02",

  rows_before = nrow(D01),

  rows_in_D02 = nrow(D02),

  rows_after = nrow(integrated),

  people_without_D02_match = sum(is.na(integrated$education_level_code)),

  columns_after = ncol(integrated),

  columns_expected = ncol(D01) + ncol(D02) - 2 #The two key columns appear once
)
```

```{r}
#| label: Join D03

integrated_rows_before_D03 <- nrow(integrated)

integrated <- integrated |>
  left_join(D03, by = c("household_id", "person_number"), relationship = "one-to-one", unmatched = "error")

#employment_status2code has no missing values in D03, so a missing value here would mean a person without a D03 match
tibble(
  join = "+ D03",

  rows_before = integrated_rows_before_D03,

  rows_in_D03 = nrow(D03),

  rows_after = nrow(integrated),

  people_without_D03_match = sum(is.na(integrated$employment_status2code)),

  columns_after = ncol(integrated),

  columns_expected = ncol(D01) + ncol(D02) - 2 + ncol(D03) - 2
)
```

```{r}
#| label: Join D08

integrated_rows_before_D08 <- nrow(integrated)

integrated <- integrated |>
  left_join(D08, by = "household_id", relationship = "many-to-one")

#computer_asset_code has no missing values in D08, so a missing value here would mean a person without a D08 match
tibble(
  join = "+ D08",

  rows_before = integrated_rows_before_D08,

  rows_in_D08 = nrow(D08),

  rows_after = nrow(integrated),

  people_without_D08_match = sum(is.na(integrated$computer_asset_code)),

  households_in_integrated_data = n_distinct(integrated$household_id),

  D08_households_not_joined = nrow(D08) - n_distinct(integrated$household_id),

  columns_after = ncol(integrated),

  columns_expected = ncol(D01) + ncol(D02) - 2 + ncol(D03) - 2 + ncol(D08) - 1
)
```

**Effect:** the row count stays at `r format(nrow(integrated), big.mark = ",")` through all three joins, so no person is duplicated or lost. Every person matches a D02, D03 and D08 record, and no columns are duplicated. The only records not carried into the person-level dataset are the `r format(nrow(D08) - n_distinct(integrated$household_id), big.mark = ",")` households with no working-age member.

## 9.3 Validation of the integrated dataset

**Problem:** matching row counts do not prove that values were attached to the right people. A join on corrupted keys (for example, IDs rounded to 15 digits as described in 1.1) could keep the row count while attaching one household's values to another.

**Treatment:** check the integrated dataset against its sources. Every person key must appear once, and no suffixed duplicate columns (`.x`/`.y`) may exist. Each household's members must share a single D08 record. The category counts must equal those in the source datasets: per person for D01, D02 and D03 columns, and per household for D08 columns.

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Integrated Dataset Checks

tibble(
  rows = nrow(integrated),

  distinct_person_keys = nrow(distinct(integrated, household_id, person_number)),

  columns = ncol(integrated),

  suffixed_duplicate_columns = sum(str_detect(names(integrated), "\\.x$|\\.y$")),

  households = n_distinct(integrated$household_id),

  households_with_one_D08_record = nrow(distinct(integrated, household_id, fixed_internet_code, mobile_internet_code,
                                                 computer_asset_code, household_smartphones))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: Values Carried Through Unchanged

D08_matched_households <- semi_join(D08, D01, by = "household_id")

tibble(
  column = c("sex (D01, per person)", "age (D01, per person)", "education_level (D02, per person)",
             "education_attendance (D02, per person)", "employment_status (D03, per person)", "salary_status (D03, per person)",
             "fixed_internet (D08, per household)", "mobile_internet (D08, per household)",
             "computer_asset (D08, per household)", "household_smartphones (D08, per household)"),

  identical_to_source = c(identical(count(integrated, sex), count(D01, sex)),
                          identical(count(integrated, age), count(D01, age)),
                          identical(count(integrated, education_level), count(D02, education_level)),
                          identical(count(integrated, education_attendance), count(D02, education_attendance)),
                          identical(count(integrated, employment_status), count(D03, employment_status)),
                          identical(count(integrated, salary_status), count(D03, salary_status)),
                          identical(count(distinct(integrated, household_id, fixed_internet), fixed_internet), count(D08_matched_households, fixed_internet)),
                          identical(count(distinct(integrated, household_id, mobile_internet), mobile_internet), count(D08_matched_households, mobile_internet)),
                          identical(count(distinct(integrated, household_id, computer_asset), computer_asset), count(D08_matched_households, computer_asset)),
                          identical(count(distinct(integrated, household_id, household_smartphones), household_smartphones),
                                    count(D08_matched_households, household_smartphones)))
)
```

**Effect:** the integrated dataset has `r format(nrow(integrated), big.mark = ",")` rows, one per working-age person, and `r ncol(integrated)` columns from D01, D02, D03 and D08. It covers `r format(n_distinct(integrated$household_id), big.mark = ",")` households, and every category count matches its source, so no value was duplicated or lost. Every join matched on complete, 18-digit keys, so each value belongs to the person or household it came from. Household-level values are repeated for each working-age member of the household, which is correct at the person grain. `person_weight` is the matching survey weight at this grain; `household_weight` was dropped in section 3.

# 10. Feature Engineering, Transformation and Encoding

The Milestone 1 analytics goal is to model employment status from education level, digital access and the interaction between the two, controlling for demographic and geographic factors, with a logistic regression and a tree-based method. This section turns the integrated dataset from section 9 into features for that goal:

- 10.1 removes the traceability flags.
- 10.2 recodes the yes/no columns to 0/1.
- 10.3 builds the engineered features.
- 10.4 applies the transformations and creates the modelling dataset.
- 10.5 encodes the modelling dataset for the two model types.
- 10.6 saves the analytical datasets.

Every rule in this section is fixed in advance: a code mapping, a constant or a threshold. Nothing is estimated from the data as a whole, so these steps can run before the train/test split in Task 4 without leaking information from test rows into training rows.

## 10.1 Remove the traceability flags

**Problem:** the `_flag` columns record which values were repaired in sections 2–7. They were needed for the verification tables above, but they are not predictors, and a model could learn the repair pattern instead of a real relationship.

**Treatment:** remove every column ending in `_flag` from the integrated dataset. The repairs remain documented in sections 2–7.

```{r}
#| label: Remove Flag Columns

flag_columns <- str_subset(names(integrated), "_flag$")

analytical <- integrated |> select(-ends_with("_flag"))

tibble(
  rows_before = nrow(integrated),

  rows_after = nrow(analytical),

  columns_before = ncol(integrated),

  columns_after = ncol(analytical),

  flag_columns_removed = paste(flag_columns, collapse = ", "),

  flag_columns_remaining = sum(str_ends(names(analytical), "_flag"))
)
```

**Effect / Verification:** `r length(flag_columns)` flag columns are removed and no rows are lost. The analytical dataset starts with `r ncol(analytical)` columns.

## 10.2 Recode yes/no columns to 0/1

**Problem:** the source codes yes/no questions as 1 = Yes and 2 = No, and the label factors from section 6 put "Yes" first. Used directly, `as.numeric()` would give 1 and 2 instead of 1 and 0, and a model would treat "Yes" as the baseline, which flips every odds ratio.

**Treatment:** create a 0/1 integer column for each yes/no variable, with 1 = Yes and 0 = No, and 1 = Female for sex. Codes classified as non-response in section 4 (9) and missing codes stay `NA`. The original `_code` and label columns are not changed.

```{r}
#| label: Recode Yes No Columns

#case_when() returns NA for any code not listed, so non-response codes stay missing
analytical <- analytical |>
  mutate(
    female = case_when(sex_code == 2 ~ 1L, sex_code == 1 ~ 0L),

    has_fixed_internet = case_when(fixed_internet_code == 1 ~ 1L, fixed_internet_code == 2 ~ 0L),

    has_mobile_internet = case_when(mobile_internet_code == 1 ~ 1L, mobile_internet_code == 2 ~ 0L),

    has_computer = case_when(computer_asset_code == 1 ~ 1L, computer_asset_code == 2 ~ 0L)
  )
```

**Verification:** every code maps to exactly one 0/1 value.

```{r}
#| label: Recode Yes No Verification

analytical |> count(sex_code, sex, female)
analytical |> count(fixed_internet_code, fixed_internet, has_fixed_internet)
analytical |> count(mobile_internet_code, mobile_internet, has_mobile_internet)
analytical |> count(computer_asset_code, computer_asset, has_computer)
```

**Effect:** four 0/1 columns are added. 1 always means "Yes" (or Female), so model coefficients read in the natural direction.

## 10.3 Engineered features

Each feature below is justified with the employment pattern it captures. The helper function summarises this pattern for every level of a feature, using `person_weight` so that each person counts for the number of people they represent:

- `percent_employed`: the share employed among all people aged 15–64.
- `employment_rate_in_labour_force`: the share employed among people who are employed or unemployed, which is the modelling target in 10.4.

```{r}
#| label: Employment Share Helper

#Weighted employment percentages for each level of a feature (used only to justify features)
employment_share <- function(data, feature) {
  data |>
    group_by({{ feature }}) |>
    summarise(
      people = n(),

      percent_employed = round(sum(person_weight[employment_status == "Employed"]) / sum(person_weight) * 100, 1),

      employment_rate_in_labour_force = round(sum(person_weight[employment_status == "Employed"]) /
                                                sum(person_weight[employment_status != "Not economically active"]) * 100, 1),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}
```

### 10.3.1 Education: `education_band` and `matric_plus`

**Problem:** `education_level` has 31 levels, many with very few people, and its level order is the dictionary order rather than a ranking (section 6). A model cannot estimate reliable effects for tiny levels, and the hypotheses are about levels of education, not individual certificates.

**Treatment:**

- `education_band` groups explicit codes into six ordered stages of education. Codes 13–15 (NTC I–III) and 19–20 (certificate or diploma without Grade 12) are below matric, so they join "Some secondary". Code 28 ("Other") is too small to stand alone and cannot be ranked, so it joins the codes classified as non-response in section 4 (29 and 99) in "Other/unknown".
- `matric_plus` is 1 for matric or any post-school qualification and 0 below matric. It is `NA` for "Other/unknown", because that education level cannot be placed above or below matric.

```{r}
#| label: Education Features

#Codes that are not listed would become NA, and the verification below confirms there are none
analytical <- analytical |>
  mutate(
    education_band = case_when(
      education_level_code == 98 ~ "No schooling",
      education_level_code %in% 0:7 ~ "Primary (Grade R-7)",
      education_level_code %in% c(8:11, 13:15, 19:20) ~ "Some secondary",
      education_level_code == 12 ~ "Matric",
      education_level_code %in% c(16:18, 21:22) ~ "Post-school certificate/diploma",
      education_level_code %in% 23:27 ~ "Degree",
      education_level_code %in% c(28, 29, 99) ~ "Other/unknown"
    ),

    education_band = factor(education_band, levels = c("No schooling", "Primary (Grade R-7)", "Some secondary", "Matric",
                                                        "Post-school certificate/diploma", "Degree", "Other/unknown")),

    matric_plus = case_when(
      education_level_code %in% c(12, 16:18, 21:27) ~ 1L,
      education_level_code %in% c(98, 0:11, 13:15, 19:20) ~ 0L
    )
  )
```

**Verification:** every education code belongs to exactly one band, and `matric_plus` agrees with the bands.

```{r}
#| label: Education Features Verification

analytical |>
  group_by(education_band, matric_plus) |>
  summarise(education_level_codes = paste(sort(unique(education_level_code)), collapse = ", "), people = n(), .groups = "drop")

tibble(people_without_a_band = sum(is.na(analytical$education_band)))

employment_share(analytical, education_band)
```

**Effect:** 31 sparse education levels become `r nlevels(analytical$education_band)` bands, and no person is left without a band. Below matric the three bands have similar employment percentages, and from matric upward the percentage rises sharply with every band. This break at matric is why `matric_plus` is used as the single education term in the interaction with digital access. In the labour force, the lowest bands show higher employment rates than "Some secondary". These bands contain mostly older people, and few of them are in the labour force, so this reflects age rather than education. It is one reason age is controlled for in the model (10.4, T2).

### 10.3.2 Digital access: `any_home_internet` and `digital_access_score`

**Problem:** digital access is spread over four columns. Mobile internet is very common, so on its own it separates people poorly, while fixed internet and computers are rare. A single yes/no hides how much access a household has, and four separate columns make the interaction test hard to read.

**Treatment:**

- `any_home_internet` is 1 if the household has fixed or mobile internet, and 0 only if both are "No". It is `NA` if one is "No" and the other is missing.
- `digital_access_score` counts the forms of access the household has: fixed internet, mobile internet, a computer and at least one smartphone (0–4). It is `NA` if any of the four is missing.

```{r}
#| label: Digital Access Features

analytical <- analytical |>
  mutate(
    any_home_internet = case_when(
      has_fixed_internet == 1 | has_mobile_internet == 1 ~ 1L,
      has_fixed_internet == 0 & has_mobile_internet == 0 ~ 0L
    ),

    digital_access_score = has_fixed_internet + has_mobile_internet + has_computer + as.integer(household_smartphones >= 1)
  )
```

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Digital Access Features Verification

analytical |> count(has_fixed_internet, has_mobile_internet, any_home_internet)

analytical |> count(digital_access_score)

employment_share(analytical, any_home_internet)

employment_share(analytical, digital_access_score)
```

**Effect:** `any_home_internet` is 1 only when at least one internet column is "Yes", and 0 only when both are "No". `digital_access_score` is missing for `r sum(is.na(analytical$digital_access_score))` people whose household has a missing digital answer. The weighted employment percentages rise with the score, with the largest increases at scores 3 and 4, so the score captures a gradient that a single yes/no column hides.

### 10.3.3 Education × digital access: `edu_digital_group`

**Problem:** the central question is whether internet access strengthens the effect of education on employment (reinforcement) or replaces it (substitution). A logistic regression tests this with the interaction term `matric_plus * any_home_internet`. Tree models and Power BI need the combination as a single column.

**Treatment:** combine `matric_plus` and `any_home_internet` into four groups. People whose education is "Other/unknown" get their own level, so they are not silently dropped. The group is `NA` only when internet access is unknown.

```{r}
#| label: Education Digital Interaction Feature

analytical <- analytical |>
  mutate(
    edu_digital_group = case_when(
      is.na(any_home_internet) ~ NA_character_,
      is.na(matric_plus) ~ "Education unknown",
      matric_plus == 0 & any_home_internet == 0 ~ "Below matric, no internet",
      matric_plus == 0 & any_home_internet == 1 ~ "Below matric, internet",
      matric_plus == 1 & any_home_internet == 0 ~ "Matric+, no internet",
      matric_plus == 1 & any_home_internet == 1 ~ "Matric+, internet"
    ),

    edu_digital_group = factor(edu_digital_group, levels = c("Below matric, no internet", "Below matric, internet",
                                                              "Matric+, no internet", "Matric+, internet", "Education unknown"))
  )
```

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Education Digital Interaction Verification

analytical |> count(matric_plus, any_home_internet, edu_digital_group)

edu_digital_rates <- employment_share(analytical, edu_digital_group)
edu_digital_rates

#Difference in the labour-force employment rate between people with and without internet, within each education group
internet_gap <- tibble(
  internet_gap_below_matric = edu_digital_rates$employment_rate_in_labour_force[edu_digital_rates$edu_digital_group %in% "Below matric, internet"] -
    edu_digital_rates$employment_rate_in_labour_force[edu_digital_rates$edu_digital_group %in% "Below matric, no internet"],

  internet_gap_matric_plus = edu_digital_rates$employment_rate_in_labour_force[edu_digital_rates$edu_digital_group %in% "Matric+, internet"] -
    edu_digital_rates$employment_rate_in_labour_force[edu_digital_rates$edu_digital_group %in% "Matric+, no internet"]
)
internet_gap
```

**Effect:** each combination of `matric_plus` and `any_home_internet` maps to exactly one group. In the labour force, people with internet have an employment rate `r internet_gap$internet_gap_below_matric` percentage points higher than those without it below matric, and `r internet_gap$internet_gap_matric_plus` points higher at matric or above. Internet is associated with a larger employment advantage for people with matric, the reinforcing pattern described in Milestone 1. The interaction term tests whether this difference between the two gaps is real. This section only builds the feature; whether the difference is statistically significant is tested in Milestone 3.

### 10.3.4 Location and age group: `settlement_type` and `youth`

**Problem:** `geo_type` and `metro` describe one thing, where a person lives, in two overlapping columns. Some combinations are very small (metro farms and metro traditional areas). The policy discussion also refers to youth, which no column identifies.

**Treatment:**

- `settlement_type` combines the two columns into four levels. Traditional areas and farms keep their own level whether or not they fall inside a metro, and urban areas are split into metro and non-metro.
- `youth` is 1 for ages 15–34, the South African youth definition, for reporting in Power BI.

```{r}
#| label: Location And Youth Features

analytical <- analytical |>
  mutate(
    settlement_type = case_when(
      geo_type_code == 2 ~ "Traditional",
      geo_type_code == 3 ~ "Farms",
      geo_type_code == 1 & metro_indicator == 1 ~ "Metro urban",
      geo_type_code == 1 & metro_indicator == 2 ~ "Non-metro urban"
    ),

    settlement_type = factor(settlement_type, levels = c("Metro urban", "Non-metro urban", "Traditional", "Farms")),

    youth = as.integer(age <= 34)
  )
```

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Location And Youth Verification

analytical |> count(geo_type, metro, settlement_type)

analytical |> group_by(youth) |> summarise(min_age = min(age), max_age = max(age), people = n())

employment_share(analytical, settlement_type)
```

**Effect:** every combination of `geo_type` and `metro` maps to one settlement type, with no missing values. The employment percentages differ clearly between settlement types, so the combined column keeps the location signal in one variable.

### 10.3.5 Household features

**Problem:** employment also depends on a person's household. Caring for children or older family members can keep people, especially women, out of work, and a household with educated members may help someone find work. Smartphone counts also mean little without household size: three phones for one person is not the same as three phones for eight people. None of these are measured directly.

**Treatment:** join `household_composition` (counted in section 5 before the age filter) many-to-one on `household_id`, then build:

- `n_working_age`: the number of people aged 15–64 in the household.
- `elderly_in_household`: 1 if anyone aged 65+ lives in the household.
- `dependency_ratio`: (children + people aged 65+) ÷ working-age members.
- `female_x_children`: `female` × `n_children_under15`, so the effect of children can differ between women and men.
- `smartphones_per_member`: smartphones ÷ all household members.
- `smartphone_access`: the ratio grouped as "None", "Fewer than 1 per member" or "1 or more per member".
- `other_member_matric`: whether another working-age member of the household has matric or higher. Members with unknown education count as not having matric.

```{r}
#| label: Household Features

analytical_rows_before_household_join <- nrow(analytical)

analytical <- analytical |>
  left_join(household_composition, by = "household_id", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  add_count(household_id, name = "n_working_age") |>
  group_by(household_id) |>
  mutate(matric_members_in_household = sum(matric_plus == 1, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    elderly_in_household = as.integer(n_elderly_65plus > 0),

    dependency_ratio = (n_children_under15 + n_elderly_65plus) / n_working_age,

    female_x_children = female * n_children_under15,

    smartphones_per_member = household_smartphones / household_size,

    smartphone_access = case_when(
      household_smartphones == 0 ~ "None",
      smartphones_per_member < 1 ~ "Fewer than 1 per member",
      smartphones_per_member >= 1 ~ "1 or more per member"
    ),

    smartphone_access = factor(smartphone_access, levels = c("None", "Fewer than 1 per member", "1 or more per member")),

    #Subtract the person's own matric so only other members are counted
    other_member_matric = case_when(
      n_working_age == 1 ~ "No other working-age member",
      matric_members_in_household - coalesce(matric_plus, 0L) > 0 ~ "Yes",
      .default = "No"
    ),

    other_member_matric = factor(other_member_matric, levels = c("No", "Yes", "No other working-age member"))
  ) |>
  select(-matric_members_in_household)
```

**Verification:** the join must not add or lose people. Every household size must equal its children plus working-age members plus people aged 65+.

```{r}
#| label: Household Features Verification

tibble(
  rows_before_join = analytical_rows_before_household_join,

  rows_after_join = nrow(analytical),

  people_without_household_composition = sum(is.na(analytical$household_size)),

  household_size_equals_sum_of_age_groups = all(analytical$household_size ==
                                                  analytical$n_children_under15 + analytical$n_working_age + analytical$n_elderly_65plus),

  smallest_dependency_ratio = min(analytical$dependency_ratio),

  largest_dependency_ratio = max(analytical$dependency_ratio),

  highest_smartphones_per_member = max(analytical$smartphones_per_member, na.rm = TRUE)
)

analytical |> count(smartphone_access)

employment_share(mutate(analytical, children = pmin(n_children_under15, 3)), children)

#Children and employment for women and men aged 25-54, the reason for female_x_children
analytical |>
  filter(between(age, 25, 54)) |>
  mutate(children = pmin(n_children_under15, 3)) |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  group_modify(~ employment_share(.x, children)) |>
  ungroup()

employment_share(analytical, elderly_in_household)

employment_share(analytical, smartphone_access)

employment_share(analytical, other_member_matric)
```

**Effect:** the row count stays at `r format(nrow(analytical), big.mark = ",")`, every person receives their household's composition, and every household size equals the sum of its age groups. The tables show the patterns these features capture: employment falls as the number of children rises, and more steeply for women than for men. Smartphone access and an educated household member are also associated with employment. `smartphone_access` is missing only for households whose smartphone count was set to missing in section 7.2.

## 10.4 Transformations

### T1 Target population: the labour force

**Problem:** `employment_status` has three levels. "Not economically active" is largely made up of students and people close to retirement, who are not looking for work, so the digital job-search mechanism in the business problem does not apply to them. A binary target also gives the odds ratios required by the technical success criteria.

**Treatment:** the modelling dataset keeps only the labour force, people who are employed or unemployed. The target `employed` is created and encoded in 10.5. The full working-age population stays in `analytical` for description and Power BI.

### T2 Centred age and age squared

**Problem:** employment does not change with age in a straight line. A single age term can only fit a straight line, and `age` and `age²` are almost perfectly correlated, which makes their regression coefficients unstable.

**Treatment:** subtract a fixed 40 from age (close to the middle of the 15–64 range) to create `age_centred`, then square it to create `age_centred_squared`. A fixed constant is used instead of the sample mean, so nothing is estimated from the data and the step cannot leak test information into training. Tree models can use `age_centred` directly, because centring does not change the order of ages.

```{r}
#| label: Centre Age

analytical <- analytical |>
  mutate(
    age_centred = age - 40,

    age_centred_squared = age_centred^2
  )
```

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Centre Age Verification

tibble(
  correlation_age_with_age_squared = round(cor(analytical$age, analytical$age^2), 3),

  correlation_centred_age_with_its_square = round(cor(analytical$age_centred, analytical$age_centred_squared), 3),

  min_age_centred = min(analytical$age_centred),

  max_age_centred = max(analytical$age_centred)
)

analytical |>
  mutate(age_band = cut(age, breaks = c(14, 24, 34, 44, 54, 64), labels = c("15-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64"))) |>
  employment_share(age_band)
```

**Effect:** centring reduces the correlation between the age terms from `r round(cor(analytical$age, analytical$age^2), 3)` to `r round(cor(analytical$age_centred, analytical$age_centred_squared), 3)`. The age bands show why a curve is needed. Among all 15–64s, employment rises until 45–54 and then falls. In the labour force, the rate jumps from 15–24 to 25–34 and then increases more slowly. Neither pattern is a straight line, and the squared term lets a logistic regression fit the curve.

### T6 Log salary (income question only)

**Problem:** reported salaries are strongly right-skewed (section 7.3). A few very high salaries would dominate an income model, and the business success criteria ask whether internet access is associated with higher income among people who report it.

**Treatment:** `log_salary` is the natural log of `salary` for employed people with a reported salary of at least R100. Section 7.3 found that values under R100 cannot plausibly be a monthly salary. Everyone else gets `NA`. `salary` itself is not changed.

```{r}
#| label: Log Salary

analytical <- analytical |>
  mutate(log_salary = if_else(employment_status == "Employed" & salary_status == "Reported" & salary >= 100, log(salary), NA_real_))
```

**Verification:**

```{r}
#| label: Log Salary Verification

analytical |>
  filter(!is.na(log_salary)) |>
  summarise(
    people = n(),

    salary_mean = round(mean(salary)),

    salary_median = median(salary),

    salary_mean_divided_by_median = round(mean(salary) / median(salary), 2),

    log_salary_mean = round(mean(log_salary), 2),

    log_salary_median = round(median(log_salary), 2)
  )

analytical |>
  filter(!is.na(log_salary)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log_salary)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(title = "Log salary (employed people with a reported salary of R100 or more)", x = "log(salary)", y = "Count")
```

**Effect:** on the Rand scale the mean is about twice the median, a sign of strong skew. On the log scale the mean and median almost coincide and the histogram is roughly bell-shaped, so no small group of high earners dominates the income model. The spikes in the histogram are most likely round amounts that respondents report (for example R5,000 or R10,000). They are genuine answers and are left unchanged.

### T3, T4, T5 and leakage: build the modelling dataset

**Problem:** the modelling dataset must contain only the target population (T1), usable predictors and no leakage. Some columns reveal the outcome directly:

- `reason_not_attending` = "Working" can only be answered by someone who works.
- The salary columns exist only for employed people.

The evidence is below.

```{r}
#| label: Leakage Evidence

analytical |>
  filter(employment_status != "Not economically active") |>
  mutate(reason_not_attending_is_working = reason_not_attending == "Working (at home, business or job)") |>
  count(reason_not_attending_is_working, employment_status) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = employment_status, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

analytical |>
  filter(employment_status != "Not economically active") |>
  count(salary_status, employment_status) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = employment_status, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

**Treatment:**

- **T1:** keep the labour force only.
- **T3:** unknown education is already kept as the "Other/unknown" level of `education_band` (10.3.1), because those people are not missing at random and dropping them would bias the sample.
- **T4:** drop the few people whose household has a missing digital-access answer. There is no dictionary code to assign, and they are too few to justify an imputation model.
- **T5:** rare levels were already merged by fixed rules in 10.3: "Other" education into "Other/unknown", and metro farms and traditional areas into "Farms" and "Traditional". No level is merged based on counts in the data.
- **Leakage:** keep only the target, the predictors and two design columns. `household_id` is needed for the household-grouped train/test split in Task 4, and `person_weight` is the survey weight. Neither is used as a predictor.

```{r}
#| label: Build Model Data

labour_force_rows <- sum(analytical$employment_status != "Not economically active")

model_data <- analytical |>
  filter(employment_status %in% c("Employed", "Unemployed")) |>
  filter(!is.na(any_home_internet), !is.na(digital_access_score)) |>
  transmute(
    #Design columns: household-grouped split and survey weights in Task 4, never predictors
    household_id, person_weight,

    #Target
    employed = employment_status,

    #Demographic and location predictors
    age_centred, age_centred_squared, female, population_group, province, settlement_type,

    #Education predictors
    education_band, matric_plus,

    #Digital access predictors
    has_fixed_internet, has_mobile_internet, has_computer, any_home_internet, digital_access_score, smartphone_access,

    #Education x digital access
    edu_digital_group,

    #Household predictors
    household_size, n_children_under15, elderly_in_household, dependency_ratio, female_x_children, other_member_matric
  )
```

**Verification:** row counts at each step, remaining missing values, and a documented reason for every column that is left out.

```{r}
#| label: Model Data Verification

tibble(
  working_age_people = nrow(analytical),

  labour_force = labour_force_rows,

  dropped_for_missing_digital_access = labour_force_rows - nrow(model_data),

  rows_in_model_data = nrow(model_data),

  columns_in_model_data = ncol(model_data),

  missing_values_excluding_matric_plus = sum(is.na(select(model_data, -matric_plus))),

  missing_matric_plus = sum(is.na(model_data$matric_plus)),

  employed = sum(model_data$employed == "Employed"),

  unemployed = sum(model_data$employed == "Unemployed"),

  percent_employed = round(mean(model_data$employed == "Employed") * 100, 1)
)

excluded_columns <- tibble(column = setdiff(names(analytical), names(model_data))) |>
  mutate(
    reason = case_when(
      column %in% c("reason_not_attending", "reason_not_attending_code", "lab_salary_raw", "salary", "salary_status", "log_salary") ~ "Leakage: reveals the employment outcome (log_salary is used in income_data)",

      column == "employment_status" ~ "Target: kept as employed",

      column %in% c("person_number", "psu") ~ "Identifier or survey design column",

      str_ends(column, "_code") | column %in% c("employment_status2code", "metro_indicator") ~ "Code column: its label or an engineered feature is used instead",

      column == "education_level" ~ "Replaced by education_band (31 sparse levels)",

      column == "sex" ~ "Replaced by female (0/1)",

      column %in% c("geo_type", "metro") ~ "Replaced by settlement_type",

      column == "age" ~ "Replaced by age_centred and age_centred_squared",

      column == "youth" ~ "Reporting group for Power BI; duplicates age in a model",

      column %in% c("fixed_internet", "mobile_internet", "computer_asset") ~ "Replaced by its 0/1 version",

      column %in% c("household_smartphones", "smartphones_per_member") ~ "Replaced by smartphone_access",

      column %in% c("n_elderly_65plus", "n_working_age") ~ "Used to build elderly_in_household and dependency_ratio",

      column %in% c("education_attendance", "institution_type") ~ "Current study status: mostly outside the labour force, kept for description",

      TRUE ~ "NOT CLASSIFIED" #Should never appear; shows up if an excluded column has no reason
    )
  )

excluded_columns |>
  group_by(reason) |>
  summarise(columns = paste(column, collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop")
```

**Effect:** the modelling dataset has `r format(nrow(model_data), big.mark = ",")` people from a labour force of `r format(labour_force_rows, big.mark = ",")`, so `r labour_force_rows - nrow(model_data)` people were dropped for missing digital access. `r round(mean(model_data$employed == "Employed") * 100, 1)`% are employed, a moderate imbalance that Task 4 should keep in mind when choosing the split and evaluation metrics. The leakage tables show that "Working" as a reason for not studying and a reported salary occur almost only among the employed, so these columns are excluded. The only missing values left are in `matric_plus`, for people with "Other/unknown" education; `education_band` and `edu_digital_group` keep these people as their own level. `r sum(excluded_columns$reason == "NOT CLASSIFIED")` excluded columns lack a documented reason.

### T7 No scaling

**Problem:** scaling puts numeric predictors on a common range. It is required for distance-based or penalised methods such as k-nearest neighbours, k-means or lasso, but not for the methods chosen in Milestone 1.

**Treatment:** no scaling is applied. Logistic regression coefficients are simply expressed per unit of each predictor, and tree-based methods split on the order of values, which scaling does not change. `person_weight` is a survey weight and must never be scaled.

```{r}
#| label: No Scaling Verification

tibble(
  person_weight_unchanged_since_integration = identical(analytical$person_weight, integrated$person_weight),

  age_centred_range = paste(range(model_data$age_centred), collapse = " to "),

  household_size_range = paste(range(model_data$household_size), collapse = " to ")
)
```

**Effect:** numeric predictors keep their natural units (years, people, ratios), which keeps the odds ratios in Milestone 3 directly interpretable.

## 10.5 Encoding for modelling

**Problem:** R's model functions encode categories automatically, but they need to be told what to compare against. By default the first factor level is the reference, and the first level of `employment_status` is "Employed". A logistic regression would therefore predict the chance of being *unemployed*. Ordered factors would make R use polynomial contrasts, which do not give readable odds ratios.

**Treatment:**

- **E1:** `employed` is a factor with "Unemployed" first, so models predict the probability of being employed.
- **E2:** the yes/no columns are already 0/1 integers (10.2).
- **E3:** each nominal factor gets a meaningful reference level, so every odds ratio reads "compared with this group":
  - `education_band`: "Some secondary", the largest group below matric.
  - `province`: Gauteng, the largest province and economic hub.
  - `population_group`: Black African, the largest group.
  - `settlement_type`: Metro urban.
  - `edu_digital_group`: "Below matric, no internet", the group with neither resource.
  - `smartphone_access`: "None".
  - `other_member_matric`: "No".
- **E4:** all factors stay unordered, so R uses treatment contrasts (each level vs the reference).
- **E5:** no manual one-hot encoding. `glm()` and `rpart()`/`randomForest()` accept factors directly and create the dummy columns internally; the `model.matrix()` output below shows this.
- **E6:** `education_level` is replaced by `education_band` (10.3.1).

```{r}
#| label: Encode Model Data

#fct_relevel() moves the named level to the front, which makes it the reference level
model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(
    employed = factor(employed, levels = c("Unemployed", "Employed")),

    education_band = fct_relevel(education_band, "Some secondary"),

    province = fct_relevel(province, "Gauteng"),

    population_group = fct_relevel(population_group, "Black African"),

    settlement_type = fct_relevel(settlement_type, "Metro urban"),

    edu_digital_group = fct_relevel(edu_digital_group, "Below matric, no internet"),

    smartphone_access = fct_relevel(smartphone_access, "None"),

    other_member_matric = fct_relevel(other_member_matric, "No")
  )
```

**Verification:** the reference level, the number of levels, whether the factor is ordered and the size of the smallest level, for every factor in the modelling dataset. The smallest level also checks T5: no level should be too small to estimate.

```{r}
#| label: Encoding Verification

model_factors <- select(model_data, where(is.factor))

tibble(
  column = names(model_factors),

  reference_level = map_chr(model_factors, ~ levels(.x)[1]),

  number_of_levels = map_int(model_factors, nlevels),

  ordered = map_lgl(model_factors, is.ordered),

  smallest_level_people = map_int(model_factors, ~ min(table(.x)))
)

model_data |> count(employed)

#E5: R creates one 0/1 column per non-reference level; the reference level (Some secondary) has no column
colnames(model.matrix(~ education_band, data = model_data))

#Column types in the final modelling dataset
enframe(map_chr(model_data, ~ class(.x)[1]), name = "column", value = "type")
```

**Effect:** `employed` has "Unemployed" as its reference, so a logistic regression models the probability of being employed. Every factor has its chosen reference level first, no factor is ordered, and the `model.matrix()` output shows that R creates the dummy columns itself, leaving out the reference level.

## 10.6 Save the analytical datasets

**Problem:** Milestone 3 needs the engineered datasets without rerunning this pipeline.

**Treatment:** save three CSV files in `Datasets/Analytical/`:

- `analytical_dataset.csv`: all `r format(nrow(analytical), big.mark = ",")` working-age people with every cleaned and engineered column, for Power BI and description.
- `model_data.csv`: the labour-force modelling dataset from 10.4–10.5.
- `income_data.csv`: employed people with a usable salary, for the internet and income question.

As in 8.2, missing values are written as empty cells. A CSV does not store factor levels, so Milestone 3 must read `household_id` as text and re-apply the level order from 10.5 after reading `model_data.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: Save Analytical Datasets

analytical_directory <- "../Datasets/Analytical/"
dir.create(analytical_directory, showWarnings = FALSE)

income_data <- analytical |>
  filter(!is.na(log_salary)) |>
  transmute(household_id, person_weight, log_salary, any_home_internet, digital_access_score, education_band, matric_plus,
            age_centred, age_centred_squared, female, population_group, province, settlement_type)

write_csv(analytical, file.path(analytical_directory, "analytical_dataset.csv"), na = "")

write_csv(model_data, file.path(analytical_directory, "model_data.csv"), na = "")

write_csv(income_data, file.path(analytical_directory, "income_data.csv"), na = "")
```

**Verification:** read the saved files back with `household_id` as text and compare them with the datasets in memory.

```{r}
#| label: Saved Analytical Datasets Verification

analytical_saved <- read_csv(file.path(analytical_directory, "analytical_dataset.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                             col_types = cols(household_id = col_character(), person_number = col_character()))

model_data_saved <- read_csv(file.path(analytical_directory, "model_data.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                             col_types = cols(household_id = col_character()))

income_data_saved <- read_csv(file.path(analytical_directory, "income_data.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                              col_types = cols(household_id = col_character()))

tibble(
  dataset = c("analytical_dataset", "model_data", "income_data"),

  rows_in_memory = c(nrow(analytical), nrow(model_data), nrow(income_data)),

  rows_in_saved_file = c(nrow(analytical_saved), nrow(model_data_saved), nrow(income_data_saved)),

  same_columns = c(identical(names(analytical_saved), names(analytical)), identical(names(model_data_saved), names(model_data)),
                   identical(names(income_data_saved), names(income_data))),

  ids_identical = c(identical(analytical_saved$household_id, analytical$household_id), identical(model_data_saved$household_id, model_data$household_id),
                    identical(income_data_saved$household_id, income_data$household_id)),

  missing_values_identical = c(sum(is.na(analytical_saved)) == sum(is.na(analytical)), sum(is.na(model_data_saved)) == sum(is.na(model_data)),
                               sum(is.na(income_data_saved)) == sum(is.na(income_data)))
)
```

**Effect:** three new files are written to `Datasets/Analytical/`. Read back with the IDs as text, each has the same rows, columns, IDs and missing values as the dataset in memory. The cleaned datasets in `Datasets/Cleaned/` and the original files in `Datasets/` are not changed by this section.
